You get a person who starts with the urgent thing. No ticket number, no queue. We answer the phone, come on-site when the fix needs hands, and keep notes so the next call does not start from zero.
We fix the parts that make the day run: email, website addresses, card readers, booking links, Wi-Fi, payments, and locked accounts.
The trade does not matter. A bar’s card reader on a Friday night. A law firm’s intake email. A clinic’s booking link. A shop’s printer. Broken is broken, and we fix it.
The goal is not to make you depend on us. Every fix gets written down in plain words, so the next change is less scary.

What we actually walk into
Card reader is down on a Friday night Payments are stuck and customers are waiting. We check the network, the device, the payment account, and any recent changes before touching anything risky.
Email stopped arriving (or stopped sending) Quotes never land, and customers think you ignored them. The cause may be a missed bill, a mail rule, or a full mailbox. We find it before guessing.

An account nobody has the password to A staff member left. The domain sits with a company nobody can name. The Google profile is tied to an old email. We map who owns what, recover what we can, and write it down.
Booking link or form is broken The worst way to find out is from a customer. We test the form, the confirmation, the email path, and where the lead is supposed to land.
Wi-Fi drops in one part of the room Sometimes it is where the router sits. Sometimes it is old gear nobody revisited. We test it where staff and customers actually stand.
A new device or account needs setup, and nobody has time New POS, printer, email, laptop, or login. The small jobs pile up. We do them, explain them, and leave the notes behind.
What people are usually wrong about
A big national IT firm will give us better support than a local shop.
A national help desk is fine for updates and monitoring. It is less useful when the POS is down, the counter is full, and someone needs to know the room.
Outsourced IT is fine if the price is right.
It can work for backups and updates. It falls short when a customer-facing tool breaks mid-service and the fix needs someone who knows your setup.
Geek Squad / corporate support is the same thing.
Retail support can fix one device. Your business has payments, booking, email, Wi-Fi, Google, and staff logins touching each other.
I’ll just Google it.
You can Google a lot of it. The risk is changing the wrong record, locking an account, or making a small problem big. Some things are worth the call.
If we have a managed-services retainer, we don’t need anyone else.
Those are different jobs. A retainer handles updates and monitoring. Local support handles the moments that need a person in your business.
Common questions
Do you help when something is broken today?
Yes. Call first if customers, payments, bookings, email, or access are hurting now. We stop the bleeding before we talk about any bigger cleanup.
Do you need passwords on the first call?
No. Never share passwords on a call or in a form. If we need access, we show you a safer way to share it. Never text, never email.
Do you require a contract or retainer?
No. We work when you need us. Regular check-ins are there if you want them. The work is hourly, scoped, and written down. You do not pay us when you do not need us.

Before recommending anything for this kind of problem, we look at what customers see, where staff repeat work, who controls the accounts, and what the business already pays for. We do not begin by selling a rebuild or another monthly tool.

What we actually walk into
Leads come in 4 ways and get tracked in 0 Calls, forms, DMs, walk-ins. Somewhere in the gaps, leads get lost. The fix is usually one simple intake list, not a giant CRM.

Reports that eat half a day You pull numbers from five places and stitch them together by hand. One simple view can save Monday morning.
A subscription that costs more than it saves A big platform for a tiny job becomes the bill nobody questions. The right move may be downgrade, connect, replace, or cancel.
Work locked in one person’s head When that person is out, the business slows down. Writing the steps down does not replace them. It makes the business less fragile.

What people are usually wrong about
We need the biggest CRM we can afford.
Usually not. Most small teams need one shared list and a few dependable next steps. A big platform earns its keep only if you keep it current. That takes people and time.
We should just use Airtable or Notion for everything.

Sometimes. Simple tools can be great at the right size. But they have limits when customer details, access, or tricky steps get involved. We tell you when one is enough and when it is only buying time.
Custom is too expensive.
Sometimes. Often the math surprises people. A subscription plus lost staff time can cost more than one focused build. The answer depends on the work, the cost, and how long you will use it.

Business software has to be clear to use.
No. Tools staff want to use save time and prevent mistakes. Care matters when people rely on a screen every day.

Customer questions, follow-up, simple reports, forms, booking, payments, staff reminders, inventory, and quotes. And when nothing fits, a small custom tool built around the job.

The bill is only one part of the cost. A cheap tool can still create work if staff copy the same detail elsewhere.
What to do first
1. Pull twelve months of card and bank charges, so yearly renewals show up. 2. Name the owner and job of each tool. 3. Mark duplicates and unused seats. 4. Test one change at a time.
When to leave it alone
Do not cancel the tool that handles payments, booking, records, or required safety rules until you know its replacement and export path.
Read each charge before you judge it

For every line on the statement, write four things: who owns the account, who uses it, when it renews, and what job it does. If nobody can name the job, mark it “investigate,” not “cancel.” Our guide to reviewing software renewals uses the same list.

A charge from apple.com/bill can cover apps, subscriptions, and other Apple purchases, Apple says. On an iPhone signed in to the Apple Account that pays, open Settings, tap your name, then tap Subscriptions.

links.text: open Settings, tap your name, then tap Subscriptions

contentBlocks.text: Can’t tell which phone or account pays? Apple suggests searching email for “receipt from Apple” or “invoice from Apple.” The receipt shows which Apple Account was used.
A tool on a personal card or personal email is a risk, even when it’s cheap. If that person leaves, the bill and the data can leave too. Move it to a business account before you trim anything.
Find the seats nobody uses
A seat, or license, is one person’s paid login. Seats pile up when staff leave and nobody tells whoever runs the account.

Google Workspace: suspending a former employee does not stop the charge. Google says suspended accounts “are still charged at the same rate as active accounts.” On the Flexible plan, deleting the account stops it. Before you delete, save their email and transfer their files, and anything only they own, to someone who stays; Google says data that isn’t transferred is permanently deleted. Google also removes the email address 20 days after deletion, so if customers still write to it, assign it to another user before then.

Google Workspace on an Annual/Fixed-Term Plan: Google says you “can't remove licenses and lower your subscription price until it's time to renew your contract.” Check your plan and renewal date before you count on a saving.

Microsoft 365 takes two moves. Remove the license from the person under Users > Active users. Then lower the count under Billing > Your products, then Remove licenses. On some billing accounts, Microsoft only lets you remove licenses within seven days of buying or renewing; after that, the subscription page shows the date the change takes effect. If that person had a phone number in Teams, Microsoft says removing the license releases it, so decide who gets that number first.
Save first. Microsoft says a removed license’s user data is held for 30 days, then permanently deleted, except documents stored in SharePoint. Export the mail and files you need before then.
Keep, downgrade, connect, or cancel
Keep it when staff use it every day and nothing else does that job well. Imperfect is fine.
Downgrade when the team uses a few features of a big plan. Compare against the vendor’s current plans page, not last year’s invoice.
Connect when staff copy the same detail from one tool into another. That copying is part of the bill.
Cancel only after you’ve downloaded your data and opened it, moved the process, and know who holds the login for whatever replaces it.

To compare options, use your own numbers for one year: the yearly charge, plus the hours spent copying (weekly minutes × 52 ÷ 60) times what an hour of that person’s time costs you. That is an estimate, not a promised saving. Sometimes the right move is to leave the bill alone.
Your next move
Bring the list to a free Tech Audit. The useful outcome can be keep, connect, replace, or leave it alone.
Quick answers
Is custom software always cheaper?
No. It has to earn its cost against the specific repeated work it removes.
Can I do this myself?
Yes. The first list is the important part; help is useful when the tools and handoffs are hard to untangle.

heading: Why is my NYC business not showing on Google Maps?
description: First check whether the business appears by name. A missing profile and a low position in a service search need different checks.
metaDescription: First check whether the business appears by name. A missing profile and a low position in a service search need different checks.

contentBlocks.text: Why is my NYC business not showing on Google Maps?
By Little Fight NYC · Published 2026-05-13 · Updated 2026-10-19
First check whether the business appears by name. A missing profile and a low position in a service search need different checks.
What this means

Search for the exact business name and location. If the profile appears there but not for a broad service search, check relevance, distance and prominence. If it is absent by name, review its verification status and any notices in the account.
What to do first

1. Search the exact business name and location. 2. Check the profile account for verification or restriction notices. 3. Compare the name, address or service area, phone, hours, category and website with the real business. 4. Follow the official guidance for the issue you find.
When to leave it alone
Do not create a second listing to fix a confusing first one. Duplicates can make a cleanup harder.
Which problem do you have?
Run these checks in order. Each one points to a different fix.

See what customers see first. Search your business name and city while signed out, or ask someone else to. Then sign in to manage it: Google says you must be signed in to the Google Account tied to the profile to find it. Search Google for “my business,” or your business name and city. Seeing it while signed in doesn’t mean customers can.
Check that it is verified. Google says only verified businesses can show their info on Maps and Search.
Look for a notice. Google says a suspended or disabled profile won’t show to other people until the issue is fixed. Here is what to do if your profile is suspended.

links.text: what to do if your profile is suspended

contentBlocks.text: Give changes time. Google says edits can take up to 3 days to appear. A new business can take up to a month to rank.
It shows by name, but not for “tailor near me”? That is ranking, not a missing profile. Google says there is no way to request or pay for a better local ranking.
Google rules to check against your listing
If those checks look fine, compare the profile with Google’s own rules.
One profile per business. Google says a duplicate won’t show on Search or Maps. If you moved, update the address on the existing profile instead of starting a new one.

A real address. A rented mailing address you don’t work from, often called a virtual office, isn’t eligible. A co-working office needs clear signage, your staff on site and customer visits during business hours.
Suite number in the right line. Google asks for the street address in Address Line 1 and the suite number in Address Line 2.
Run it from home and travel to customers? Google says to clear a home address from the profile. Set a service area instead, meaning the places you travel to.
The name on your sign. Google says unnecessary words in the business name aren’t permitted and could get the profile suspended.
When someone else controls the profile
A past employee, an old web vendor or a former owner may still hold it. Don’t start a second profile to get around them.

If nobody ever verified it, Google says you can claim and verify it. If someone else verified it and customers visit your shop or office, request ownership at business.google.com/add. Google gives the current owner 3 days to answer. If there is no reply, you may get the option to claim it. Google says that option isn’t always available. If you travel to customers and have no shop or office, Google says to contact its support instead and ask to transfer ownership of the listing.
Once it is back, keep the owner login in the business’s name. Here is how to keep your accounts yours.

links.text: how to keep your accounts yours

contentBlocks.text: When the profile is not the problem

If the profile shows by name and every fact matches the shop, stop changing the basics. Fill in anything still blank, like special hours or details such as Wi-Fi, add real photos and keep replying to reviews; Google lists each of those as a way to improve local ranking. Google says prominence draws on things like how many websites link to you and how many reviews you have. That part builds over time. Read whether local search help is worth it before paying anyone.

If the facts are right but the profile is still wrong, save screenshots and use the official support path; NYC owners can also bring that evidence to us.

A clear site helps people verify the business after they find the listing.
Can anyone guarantee a map position?
No. Be careful with that promise.

contentBlocks.text: When does a custom business system beat another subscription?
By Little Fight NYC · Published 2026-05-13 · Updated 2026-10-19
Build only when a specific repeated handoff has no good existing fit.
What this means
A custom system is useful when the business keeps paying people to bridge the same gap by hand.
What to do first
1. Trace one repeated job. 2. Mark every copy, wait, and workaround. 3. Check whether a current tool can be configured or connected. 4. Price the smallest useful change.
When to leave it alone
Do not build a custom app to replace a tool people already use successfully. That is expensive pride in a tiny tuxedo.
Go in order: keep, connect, replace, build
Each step usually asks for more money and more change than the one before. Stop at the first one that fixes the broken outcome. Name the outcome, not the tool you dislike.
Keep: the tool is clunky, but staff use it and customers aren’t hurt. Write the workaround down and move on.

Connect: two tools hold the same facts and someone retypes them. The link may already exist. Google Forms, for example, can store responses in a linked Google Sheet: open Responses, then More, then Select destination for responses. Pick one place as the record, so two copies never disagree.
Replace: the current tool blocks a must-have job. Download a copy of your data and open it before you sign anything new.
Build: the gap is specific, it happens every week, and the first three didn’t fix it. A problem that shows up twice a year rarely earns custom software.
Do the boring math first
Count one repeated job for a week. Then estimate its yearly cost with your own numbers:
Minutes per repeat × repeats per week × 52 ÷ 60 = hours a year spent bridging the gap.
Hours × the hourly cost you choose, including what that person’s time is really worth to the business.
Plus the yearly cost of every subscription that touches the job.
Set that against the full cost of building: the build, upkeep, moving data in, and moving it out later. It is an estimate, not a promised saving. If the numbers are close, keep renting.

Paper counts too. A clipboard can beat a login when one person uses it, in one place, and nobody needs a report. It starts costing time when the same fact gets copied into a calendar, a spreadsheet, and an invoice, or staff wait on one notebook. Fix the worst handoff with the smallest reliable tool, like the form-to-sheet link above.
Before you build, settle who owns it
Accounts: when we build, the accounts stay in the business’s name.

Code: the U.S. Copyright Office says copyright “initially belongs to the author(s) who created that work,” with exceptions such as an employee’s regular work. Owning a copy of the files does not give you the copyright. A transfer “generally must be made in writing and signed.” Put ownership in the written agreement and have a lawyer read it. This is not legal advice.
Upkeep: who fixes it when a phone update or vendor change breaks something, and how is that billed?
Exit: how does your data come out if you stop? See how to make sure you own your domain, website, and accounts.

title: How to Choose a Web Designer in NYC | Little Fight NYC
heading: How do I choose a web designer in NYC?
description: Judge live work, ownership, scope, and communication—not the loudest opinion.
metaDescription: Judge live work, ownership, scope, and communication—not the loudest opinion.

contentBlocks.text: How do I choose a web designer in NYC?
By Little Fight NYC · Published 2026-07-12 · Updated 2026-10-19
Judge live work, ownership, scope, and communication—not the loudest opinion.
What this means
Forum advice can surface questions, but it cannot prove that a builder fits your business.
What to do first
1. Ask for live sites. 2. Ask who does the work. 3. Get scope, timeline, access, and ownership in writing. 4. Ask what happens if the work pauses.
When to leave it alone
Do not hire from a screenshot gallery alone or hand over control of the domain to a vendor account.
Five questions to ask before you sign
Whose name is on the domain and the website account? The answer should be the business, with the designer added as a user. Here is how to own your domain name.

links.text: how to own your domain name

contentBlocks.text: Who fixes things after launch, and is that care written into the contract?
Who owns the design, words, and photos made for us? See below before you accept a vague answer.

How do you check accessibility? ADA.gov lists basics such as color contrast, alt text on images, video captions, labeled forms, and text that still works when zoomed. More in our guide to website accessibility.
What results do you promise? Google says no one can guarantee a #1 ranking on Google, and to beware of anyone who claims to.
Paying for the site is not the same as owning it

The U.S. Copyright Office says the person who creates a work is ordinarily its author. A commissioned work counts as “made for hire” only if it fits one of nine listed categories and both sides sign a written agreement saying so.

If the work does not pass every one of those tests, the designer keeps the copyright unless they transfer it. The Copyright Office says a transfer generally must be in writing and signed by the owner of the rights, which here means the designer. So the contract, signed by the designer, should say what the business owns once paid: the design, the words, photos made for you, and the right to edit or move them. Ask which parts come from a template, font, or stock photo service, and whose account pays for each.
This is not legal advice. If the ownership section is unclear, have a lawyer read it before you sign.
In New York City, put the deal in writing

Hiring a solo freelancer? City law may already require a written contract. NYC’s Freelance Isn’t Free Act says contracts worth $800 or more must be in writing. That includes agreements with the same person that add up to $800 in any 120-day period.

The contract must spell out the work, the pay, and the payment date. If it has no payment date, the city says the business must pay within 30 days after the work is done. Both sides must keep a copy. The city also publishes a model contract with the required terms. This is not legal advice; if a term is unclear, ask a lawyer.

Freelancer or agency, also get these in writing: the page list, who supplies words and photos, and rounds of changes. Add the launch date, the handoff items (logins, final files, editing notes), and how either side can end the work.
Test their work yourself, or skip the hire
Open three live sites they built on your own phone. Tap the phone number, the booking button, and the form.
If they offer a search audit, give read-only access. Google advises granting only read access to Search Console, its report on how your site shows up in search, at that stage.
Ignore cold emails promising page one. Google says to be wary of SEO firms and web consultants or agencies that email you out of the blue.

You may not need a designer at all. Google says a small local business can probably do much of its own search work. If the job is one page with hours, phone, and a booking link, a builder may be enough. Weigh Squarespace against hiring a web designer first.

links.text: Squarespace against hiring a web designer

Either can fit. Clear ownership and accountable work matter more than the label.
What must the business own?
At minimum, its domain and the access needed to run the public site.

heading: Should I use Squarespace or hire a web designer?
description: A simple DIY site can fit; hire help when the customer path or your available time does not.
metaDescription: A simple DIY site can fit; hire help when the customer path or your available time does not.

contentBlocks.text: Should I use Squarespace or hire a web designer?
By Little Fight NYC · Published 2026-07-12 · Updated 2026-10-19
A simple DIY site can fit; hire help when the customer path or your available time does not.
What this means
The platform is a tool. The decision is whether the business can finish and maintain the public job the site needs to do.
What to do first
1. List the essential pages. 2. Build the call, booking, order, or inquiry path. 3. Test it on a phone. 4. Set a realistic time limit.
When to leave it alone
Do not hire help because a template is unfashionable. Do not keep DIYing forever because the template looked easy on day one.
When doing it yourself on Squarespace is the right call
Squarespace is a fair answer for plenty of small businesses. Doing it yourself makes sense when most of these are true:
The site is a handful of pages: what you do, prices or menu, hours and location, and contact.
Booking, ordering, or payments already run through a tool you like, and the site only needs to send people there.
You have the words and photos, or can pull them together in a weekend.
Someone at the business will update hours and prices when they change.

Some upkeep comes built in. Squarespace says every domain correctly pointed at a Squarespace site gets a free SSL certificate automatically. SSL is the security layer Squarespace says helps stop hackers from stealing visitors’ information, like what a customer types into your contact form.
When hiring help is the better use of money
You started the site months ago and it is still not live.
The site has to hand information to another system, like an intake form that should land in your booking calendar or client records.
You have more than one location, service area, or language, and each needs a clear page of its own.
An hour of your time is worth more than an hour of help. Do that math honestly.
Hiring help does not have to mean leaving Squarespace. See the middle path below.
Check what comes with you if you leave later

Leaving Squarespace is possible, but not everything comes along. Squarespace’s export makes one .xml file in WordPress format, a data file built for importing into WordPress. It includes layout pages, one blog, text blocks, and image blocks. The photos themselves may not come along: Squarespace warns that some WordPress imports only link back to images stored on Squarespace, and those links stop working after you cancel. Check that every image shows up on the new site before you cancel anything.

It leaves out store pages, product blocks, video blocks, drafts, style settings, and custom CSS, the extra style code some sites use. Store products export on their own to a .csv spreadsheet file, which Squarespace says skips featured images, variant images, image alt text, and customer reviews.
So keep your own copies of final page text, photos, and logo files from day one. If booking runs inside the site, read how to move off Squarespace without breaking booking before you plan any switch.

links.text: how to move off Squarespace without breaking booking

contentBlocks.text: The middle path: a designer builds, the business owns
Set it up so the business keeps the keys:
Create the Squarespace account yourself, with a business email address and a business card on file. Do the same for the domain; here is how to own your domain name.

links.text: how to own your domain name

contentBlocks.text: Invite the designer as a contributor with Administrator permission while they build. Squarespace says administrators can do almost everything the owner can, except transfer ownership. Its permissions chart shows that includes deleting the site and canceling the subscription, so give it only for the build.

If the designer already built the site in their own account, ask for a transfer before launch. Squarespace says only the current site owner can transfer ownership, and attached Squarespace domains move with the site.
When the work ends, remove the designer or lower their access. Keep a short list of who can log in, and see our notes on keeping your accounts yours.

A platform alone does not settle that question; content, structure, and setup still matter.

Usually, but confirm content, domain, and booking handoffs before moving.

metaDescription: Yes, when it starts with accurate public facts and useful pages, not a promised position.

contentBlocks.text: Is local search work worth it for my NYC business?
By Little Fight NYC · Published 2026-07-12 · Updated 2026-10-19
Yes, when it starts with accurate public facts and useful pages, not a promised position.
What this means
A nearby customer needs clear business information and a path they can finish. Search work supports that; it does not replace it.
What to do first
1. Check the Google profile. 2. Check name, address, phone, and hours across public pages. 3. Fix broken customer paths. 4. Reply to real reviews in your own voice.
When to leave it alone
Do not buy a ranking guarantee or publish thin location pages just to catch a phrase.
Why chains seem to win the map

Local SEO is the work that helps nearby people find you on Google Maps and Search. Google says local results are mainly based on relevance, distance, and popularity. Its help page calls the third one prominence.
Relevance is how well your Business Profile matches what someone searched.
Distance is how far you are from the person searching.
Prominence means how well-known a business is. Google says links to your website and your reviews feed into it.

Chains usually start ahead on that last one. Their names are known. Head offices often keep every location’s hours and categories in sync. Google says there is no way to request or pay for a better local ranking.
Your edge is the other two. For people searching near your shop, distance helps you as much as any chain. And you can be more specific than a chain: real services, real hours, your block.
Clean up these profile details first
From Google’s own Business Profile rules:

Use your real-world name, as it appears on your sign. Google says extra words, like a tagline or a neighborhood that isn’t part of your real name, aren’t permitted. They could get the profile suspended.
Choose the fewest categories that describe your core business, as Google asks.
If you go to customers and don’t receive them, hide your address. Google gives the example of a plumber working from home.
Ask for reviews with a Google review link or QR code at the counter. Never trade a discount or freebie for one. Google calls that fake content and strictly prohibits it.
Not showing up at all? Start with why a business goes missing from Google Maps.

links.text: why a business goes missing from Google Maps

contentBlocks.text: When to pay for help, and when to skip it

Google says a small local business can probably do much of this work itself. Pay for help when the facts are tangled across several systems. Or when nobody has time to keep them current. Google also calls a redesign or new site a great time to hire help.
Skip a monthly retainer if most new customers come by referral, or you are booked out. A one-time cleanup may be enough.
If you do hire someone, Google suggests questions like these:
What results do you expect, by when, and how will you measure them?
Will you show me every change you make, and why?
Can you start with read-only access? Search Console is Google’s report on how your site shows in search. For an audit, Google says to grant read access only, not edit access.

Be wary of cold emails about your listing. Be wary of anyone who says you must link to them, or offers to submit your site to thousands of search engines. Google warns about all three. Keep the profile and website accounts in the business’s name. Then they stay with you if a vendor leaves.
How to tell if it is working

Open your Business Profile on Google, click Performance, and pick a date range. You will see calls, direction requests, website clicks, and the searches people used. The numbers only show for verified profiles.

Read them with two cautions. Google says the counts include organic results and Google Ads. If you run ads, you are not looking at free search alone. And Google counts a call each time someone clicks the call button. That is a tap, not a sale. Check the trend against your register.
Your next move
Start with the facts you control. If several systems disagree, ask for a Tech Audit.

Do ads replace local search work?
Ads and organic visibility are different tools. Neither fixes wrong public facts.
How fast will it work?
There is no safe universal timeline; judge the quality of the setup and evidence over time.

contentBlocks.text: What should I fix on my Google Business Profile?
By Little Fight NYC · Published 2026-07-12 · Updated 2026-10-19
Use the official profile rules before copying a tip from a thread.
What this means
A profile is public business information. Small errors can confuse customers; shortcuts can create a bigger cleanup.
What to do first
1. Check ownership and verification. 2. Correct category, hours, phone, services, and website. 3. Add accurate photos. 4. Reply to real reviews without scripting a fake conversation.
When to leave it alone
Do not create duplicates, stuff keywords into the name, or offer rewards for reviews.
Setting up or claiming the profile
Search your business name and city on Google Maps first. What you find decides the next step.
Nothing there: add it at business.google.com/add. Google says adding or claiming a profile is free.
A profile exists but nobody verified it: open it in Google Maps and select Claim this business.
A past employee or vendor verified it: request ownership from the current owner. Don’t make a second profile.
Google picks the verification methods, and you can’t change them. Options can include phone or text, email, a live video call or a postcard.
Phone: Google says automated phone menus, the “press 1 for hours” kind, won’t get the code. Answer the line live or pick text.
Video: be at the shop. Google suggests showing outside signs, your equipment, and an employee-only area or your keys.
Postcard: don’t edit the name, address or category while you wait, and don’t request a new code. Codes expire after 30 days.
Google says its review takes up to 5 business days, sometimes longer. Google will never ask for your code, so don’t read it to anyone who calls.
Fix the facts the way Google’s rules read
Name: use the name on your sign, website and stationery. Leave out taglines, hours, phone numbers and service keywords. Google says extra words could get the profile suspended.
Category: pick the fewest that describe the core business. Google’s test is “this business IS a,” not “this business HAS a.”
Hours: list the hours customers can come in, and set special hours for holidays. Google says appointment-only businesses shouldn’t list hours.
Phone: use a number the business controls. Google prefers a local number over a call center line.
Description: no links and no sale prices. Google doesn’t allow either there.

Google can also pick up category details from your website. Keep the site and profile saying the same thing. After any change, test it like a customer: tap call, directions and the website link. Here is what Google looks for on a business website.

links.text: what Google looks for on a business website

contentBlocks.text: Give people access without giving away the profile
Don’t share one login. Google says each person should use their own Google Account, so nobody shares a password.
Make staff or a vendor a manager. Managers can edit info, reply to reviews and post. They can’t add or remove people or delete the profile.
Keep the primary owner on an account the business controls. A profile has only one primary owner.
To add or remove someone, open the profile and go to More, then Business Profile settings, then People and access.
When someone leaves, remove them there. Their past review replies and posts stay on the profile. See what to do when someone leaves the team.

links.text: what to do when someone leaves the team

contentBlocks.text: When paid help makes sense
Google notes that outside managers often charge a fee to run a profile. Walk away from anyone who promises a ranking. Google says third parties can’t promise or directly influence where you rank.

If a caller says they work for Google, Google suggests asking them to email you from an @google.com address. If you do hire help, Google suggests reviewing the profile’s performance each month. If the profile is verified, the facts match and customers call, you may not need help at all.
Your next move
Save screenshots of anything wrong, then use the official route or bring the evidence to us.
Quick answers
Should I post every day?
Use updates when they are useful to customers; do not post filler for its own sake.
Can I ask for reviews?
Ask honestly and follow Google’s policy.

title: Website Developer Disappeared? What to Do | Little Fight NYC
heading: What should I do if my website builder stops responding?
description: Secure what the business owns before trying to recover the design.
metaDescription: Secure what the business owns before trying to recover the design.

contentBlocks.text: What should I do if my website builder stops responding?
By Little Fight NYC · Published 2026-07-12 · Updated 2026-10-19
Secure what the business owns before trying to recover the design.
What this means
A stalled project is easier to handle when the domain, hosting, email, billing, files, and access are documented.
What to do first
1. Save contracts, invoices, and messages. 2. Check domain and host ownership. 3. Change access only through accounts the business controls. 4. Copy available files and backups.
When to leave it alone
Do not destroy the old site or start a public fight before preserving the evidence and access.
First, find out who holds the domain
The domain is your web address. ICANN says you must renew a domain before it expires to keep using it and the services tied to it, like a website or email. So start here.
Look up the domain at lookup.icann.org. ICANN says the “Registrar” field shows which company holds the registration.

Find out when it expires. ICANN policy requires registrars to send renewal reminders about one month and one week before expiration. If those go to the developer’s inbox, nobody at the business sees them.

If it already lapsed, call the registrar today. For .com and other generic endings, ICANN says a deleted domain enters a 30-day redemption period when it can still be restored, sometimes for an extra fee. ICANN policy says the restore is done at the request of whoever was the registrant when it expired, so if that was the developer, you will need their help. Country endings such as .us or .co can follow different rules, so ask the registrar.

If the business is the registrant, meaning the legal holder of the domain, you can move it to an account you control. A move needs an auth code, which a registrar creates to stop unauthorized transfers. If you cannot create one in the registrar’s account, ICANN says the registrar must hand it over within five calendar days of your request. Before you move it to a new registrar, screenshot the domain’s DNS settings, the records that point it at your website and email. Squarespace notes most domain hosts can’t keep those settings in place during a transfer.

If the developer is listed instead, ask them in writing to change the registrant to the business. ICANN notes that a registrant change can start a 60-day lock on moving to another registrar, though some registrars let you opt out.
Then take back the other keys
Website platform. On Squarespace, only the current site owner can transfer ownership, so the developer has to start it. Ask for it in writing, with a date. Other platforms have their own steps.

Google Business Profile. If someone else owns your verified profile, Google lets you request ownership. The current owner gets 3 days to respond. If they do not, you may get the option to claim it, though Google says that option isn’t always available.

Google Search Console, Google’s report on how your site shows up in search. After you verify ownership yourself, Google says you can unverify previous owners by removing their verification token. A token is the proof they used: a file or a line of code (an HTML tag) on the site, a record at your domain company, or their edit access to your Google Analytics or Tag Manager account. Google says an old owner can verify again while any of their tokens remain, so clear every one.
Forms, visit tracking, email, and payments. Confirm where form messages land and that the business can log in to each tool. Our list for handing off a vendor helps.
Early signs a project is losing its owner
Silence is not the only sign. Watch for these earlier ones:
Nobody at the business can log in to the domain or hosting.
Progress shows up only in screenshots, never in a working preview link.
Dates slip without a new written plan.
There is no backup, export, or handoff note.

If you see one, send a calm written request for the current status, what is finished, what is blocking the work, and a handoff date. Keep the reply with your records. We are not lawyers, and this is not legal advice. If money or the contract is in dispute, talk to a lawyer before you cut off anyone’s access.
Your next move
If you cannot tell what the business controls, bring the account list to a Tech Audit.
Quick answers
Can I get my domain back?
The answer depends on registration and proof of control; start with the registrar record.
Should I rebuild immediately?
Only after you know what is live, what is recoverable, and what the customer path needs.

contentBlocks.text: How do I choose a register and payment system?
By Little Fight NYC · Published 2026-07-12 · Updated 2026-10-19
Pick the register and payment system that fits the actual shift, staff, hardware, and customer path.
What this means
A register and payment system touches payments, devices, inventory, permissions, receipts, reporting, and sometimes online ordering.
What to do first
1. Write down the busy hour. 2. List hardware and required connections between tools. 3. Test staff permissions and refunds. 4. Check the provider’s current offline and support documentation.
When to leave it alone
Do not switch from a single bad shift or a forum poll. Diagnose whether the issue is provider, internet, hardware, or setup.
Six questions to ask every vendor in writing
Ask each vendor the same six questions. Get the answers in writing before anyone books an install.

Hardware: what you own, lease, or rent, and what you can reuse. Square’s restaurant page says hardware is not included with its subscription. It says you may be able to reuse iPads, kitchen printers, receipt printers, cash drawers, and routers. Ask every vendor about the devices you already have.

Payment processing, meaning the company that moves card money into your bank. Ask whether the register ties you to one processor. Toast’s billing FAQ says you must use Toast’s processing services. Clover’s pricing page says its devices cannot be used with other payment processors, even if bought from another seller. Ask Square too, in writing.

Offline mode, meaning taking cards while the internet is down. Ask how long stored payments last and who pays for a decline. Square’s restaurant page says offline payments are declined if you do not reconnect within 24 hours of the first one. Square’s help center says pending offline payments expire after 72 hours and cannot be recovered, and highly recommends uploading within 24 hours to cut the risk of declines and chargebacks. Plan around 24 hours. Square makes you responsible for expired, declined, or disputed offline payments. Clover says its devices can take offline payments for up to 7 days. Clover says you accept the risk of a declined or partial payment.

Contract terms: length, early-exit fees, auto-renewal, and what happens to leased hardware at the end. Clover says its hardware subscriptions are non-cancelable, though you can pay one off or upgrade. If you neither buy nor return the equipment at the end, the term extends at the same monthly charge, so Clover asks you to tell it your choice at least 30 days before the term ends. Terms and termination fees vary by the company that sold you Clover. Square’s restaurant page says its plans have no locked-in contracts. Toast’s billing FAQ points to the Toast Merchant Agreement for rates and terms.
Data export: how items, customers, sales history, and gift card balances come out if you leave. Ask for a sample file now, not on the day you cancel.
Staff workflows: who can refund, void, discount, and open the drawer. Give each person their own code, so every refund traces to a name.

If your current system passes all six, fix the setup before you switch. Start with why the card reader disconnects during service. Already down to two names? Read Toast vs. Clover for a bar or Square vs. Toast for a Manhattan restaurant.

links.text: why the card reader disconnects during service
Toast vs. Clover for a bar
Square vs. Toast for a Manhattan restaurant

contentBlocks.text: Two New York rules the register has to handle

New York City’s consumer agency, DCWP, says businesses must accept cash unless they have a machine that turns cash into a prepaid card. They cannot charge more for paying in cash. The city law allows that machine only if it charges no fee and needs no more than a one-dollar minimum, and cash must be taken whenever it is broken. Phone, mail, and online orders can be card-only unless the customer pays in the store. So plan for a cash drawer and a cash count at close. If the register rounds cash totals to the nickel, DCWP says the rounding must favor the customer and be disclosed before the sale.

Card fees have rules too. Under a New York State law, a business that adds a card fee must display the highest total price for each purchase, before sales tax, and the fee cannot be more than the card company charges the business. DCWP says a sign at the register announcing a fee on all card sales is not allowed, and neither is a fee that shows up as a line on the receipt without the total price posted first.
If a vendor offers a surcharge or cash-discount setting, read the DCWP business guidance first. This is general information, not legal advice. Talk to a lawyer about your own pricing.

Is one register and payment system best for every business?
No. The useful fit depends on the business and current process.
Can I keep my current hardware?
Check the provider’s current compatibility documentation directly.

description: Yes, if a new customer ever needs a stable place to verify you and act. Most do.
metaDescription: Yes, if a new customer ever needs a stable place to verify you and act. Most do.

contentBlocks.text: Does my small business need a website?
By Little Fight NYC · Published 2026-07-12 · Updated 2026-10-19
Yes, if a new customer ever needs a stable place to verify you and act. Most do.
What this means
Social, referrals, and a Google profile can help people discover you. A business-controlled page can hold the facts when someone needs them now.
What to do first
1. Search your business name on a phone. 2. Check whether a stranger can understand the offer. 3. Check the next action. 4. Make sure the business controls the domain and access.
When to leave it alone
Do not build a giant site if one clear page and a working action solve the real problem.
Why a Google profile alone is not enough
Your Google Business Profile is the panel with your hours, map pin, and reviews. Keep it. But you do not fully control it.

Google says it gathers business info from sources like user reports and licensed content, and may update your profile if those sources say it is wrong. Some suggested edits come to you first, and you get 4 days to accept or reject them.

If you do not answer, Google says it may publish the change when other public information, such as your business website, supports it. That cuts both ways. A current site backs up the right hours. A stale one can back up the wrong ones.
When you can skip a full website for now
Some businesses can wait. If customers all come by referral, your calendar is full, and your Google profile is right, a full site may not earn its keep yet. Three small moves still make sense:
Verify your Google profile. Google says verifying tells it you are authorized to represent the business. Our Google Business Profile tips cover the rest.
Register the domain name in the business’s own name, so it is ready when you need it.

links.text: Register the domain name in the business’s own name

contentBlocks.text: Keep one master list of name, address, phone, and hours, so every listing matches.
If social media is your only page today, read our take on Instagram instead of a website.
The smallest website that does the job
Start with one page. It should answer what a stranger wants to know before they call or walk over:
What you do, in the words a neighbor would use.
Your neighborhood or service area, your hours, and a phone number someone answers.
One main action near the top: call, book, order, or visit.
The same name, address, phone, and hours as your Google profile. Google says businesses with complete and accurate info are more likely to show up in local search results.

Then put the site on your profile. Google lets you add your website to your Business Profile, and some business categories may be able to add links for orders, reservations, or appointments. Test every link on a phone, or run the page through our website check. Fix the first dead end before you add another app.
If customers send you health, money, or legal details
Pharmacies, clinics, tax preparers, and law offices need one more layer of care. Put hours, phone, and refill or appointment links near the top, so people find them without calling.

Keep the general contact form for general questions. Send prescriptions, health details, and account numbers through the system your office already approved. title: Google Business Profile Suspended? What to Do (NYC Guide)
heading: Google Business Profile Suspended? Start Here
description: Stop random edits, read the notice, fix what it names, and use Google’s official process with real business proof.
metaDescription: Stop random edits, read the notice, fix what it names, and use Google’s official process with real business proof.

contentBlocks.text: Google Business Profile Suspended? Start Here
By Little Fight NYC · Published 2026-07-12 · Updated 2026-10-19
Stop random edits, read the notice, fix what it names, and use Google’s official process with real business proof.
What this means
A suspension can affect how public information appears. Random changes and duplicate listings can make it harder to understand what happened.
What to do first

1. Save the notice and screenshots. 2. Confirm the business facts and correct anything that breaks Google’s guidelines, starting with what the notice names. 3. Gather truthful supporting documents. 4. Follow Google’s current appeal instructions.
When to leave it alone
Do not make a replacement listing or pay someone who promises a guaranteed reinstatement.
Which notice did you get?
The fix depends on the exact problem. Read the wording before you change anything.
Profile suspended or disabled. Google sends a notification to the Google Account that manages the profile. Until it is fixed, the profile won’t show to other people on Google.

Whole account restricted. Google says every profile you manage is suspended, and you can’t create or claim others. Appeal the account first on your Google Account’s My accounts page, then appeal the profile.

Reviews restricted. Google can respond to fake or rewarded reviews by blocking new reviews for a set time. It can also hide existing reviews or show a warning. Google says it emails the owner when it plans a restriction.
Not verified. Google says an unverified profile’s content might not appear, so check verification status before you appeal.

A rejected edit, like a new name or category. Google handles that appeal through its contact form, not the appeals tool. That applies outside the UK and the European Economic Area, so it covers New York.
Fix the cause, then appeal once
Google says appeals can only be submitted once. Get everything ready before you press submit.
Open Google’s appeals tool from its page on fixing suspended profiles. It shows the date, the reason, a link to the rule involved and whether the decision can be appealed.

links.text: its page on fixing suspended profiles

contentBlocks.text: Read that rule against your profile. Google’s guidelines bar extra words in the business name, virtual office addresses and more than one profile per business. Correct what the notice names so it matches the real business. Then check the rest of the profile against the same guidelines and fix anything else that breaks them. Skip changes you don’t need, like trying a new name or category to see what sticks. Google asks that the profile follow all its guidelines before you appeal.

Gather proof. Google lists business registration, a business license, tax certificates and utility bills such as electricity, phone, water or internet. The name and address on each should match the profile.
Explain the fix in a few plain sentences. Upload the files, then confirm everything is attached and submit. Google emails the decision.

Google’s appeals page currently says decisions can take up to 5 business days. Treat that as Google’s estimate, not a promise. Don’t file a second appeal for the same issue while you wait. If it is denied, Google says it may do an additional review, with evidence you didn’t send the first time.
Keep the profile safe for next time

Check who owns the profile. Google says if it removes an owner’s Google Account, it removes every location that account owns. Keep ownership on an account the business controls, not a past vendor’s or a former employee’s. Here is how to keep your accounts yours.

links.text: how to keep your accounts yours

contentBlocks.text: If the notice names one clear rule and the fix is one field, you can file through Google’s tool yourself. If the profile is back but still hard to find, see why a business doesn’t show on Google Maps.

If Maps is important to the business, bring the notice and proof list to a Tech Audit before you submit the appeal. Google says appeals can only be submitted once, so a second look helps most before you press submit.

Can I make a new listing?
No. Google says not to create a new Business Profile for the same business. Use the official appeal process instead.
How long does an appeal take?
Do not rely on a universal timeline. Check Google’s current guidance.

title: Website Down? An Emergency Checklist for NYC Businesses
heading: Website Down? What a Small Business Should Check First
description: Find out whether the problem is the page, connection, domain, or host before changing anything.
metaDescription: Find out whether the problem is the page, connection, domain, or host before changing anything.

contentBlocks.text: Website Down? What a Small Business Should Check First
By Little Fight NYC · Published 2026-07-12 · Updated 2026-10-19
Find out whether the problem is the page, connection, domain, or host before changing anything.
Read the error before you change anything
The words on the screen point to what broke. Screenshot them. In Chrome, the short code under the message matters most.
ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED: Chrome’s help says the web address doesn’t exist or now points somewhere else. Start with the domain check below.

ERR_EMPTY_RESPONSE or ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED: the site sent nothing back or turned the visit away. Chrome says an empty response means the page “might be down”; a refused connection can also mean the page is blocked. If cellular data shows the same code, check the host next.

“Your connection is not private”: a certificate warning. A certificate is the file that lets a browser open your site over a private, secure link. If the code is NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID, check the device’s clock first; Chrome says a wrong date and time can cause it. If every device shows it, tell whoever runs the site.

“Website Expired” on a Squarespace site: the plan lapsed, not the design. Squarespace says sites expire “when we can't authorize an automatic payment or if auto-renew is disabled.” Check the card on file first.
Check the domain before anything else

Your domain is the address customers type. A registrar is the company you pay to hold it. If it lapses, the site and the email on it can stop together. ICANN, which sets the rules for .com and similar addresses, says that shutdown stops services “such as a website or email service.”
Find the registrar: search your domain at lookup.icann.org, ICANN’s lookup tool. ICANN says the registrar’s name will be in the results.

Search the inbox for renewal notices. ICANN rules require registrars to send them about one month and one week before expiry, to the owner email listed on the domain. If that inbox belongs to a former employee or old web person, read how to own your domain name later.

links.text: how to own your domain name

contentBlocks.text: Renew in that same registrar account. ICANN says that once you renew, the registrar must make the domain work again “as soon as commercially reasonable.”
Do not buy a new domain or move this one mid-outage. A deleted domain sits in a 30-day redemption period, and ICANN says the current registrar must restore it before it can be transferred.
If the domain is fine, check the host
The host is the company whose computers send your pages when a customer taps your link.

Check the host’s status page, where it posts outages. Squarespace’s guide says a site that won’t load “could be related to a system-wide issue” and points to status.squarespace.com. If an incident is posted, the fix is on their side.
Try the built-in address. Squarespace says that if the site opens at its .squarespace.com address but not at yours, that “suggests that there's an issue with your custom domain.”
Keep customers moving while it’s down

Search is rarely the emergency. Google says its systems are built “to help websites recover from temporary issues.” Do not delete the site, hide it from search, or ask Google to remove it while you fix it.

Give customers another way in. Check the phone number on your Google Business Profile. Post a short note on the social page they already use. When you call or text us, add the registrar and host names.
What this means
A site can appear down only on one connection, or it can be unavailable to everyone. Those are different problems.
What to do first
1. Check from a phone on cellular data. 2. Check a second page. 3. Check domain renewal and hosting notices. 4. Save screenshots and timestamps.
When to leave it alone
Do not point the domain somewhere new or rebuild in a panic before preserving the current access and evidence.
Your next move
If customers cannot reach a key path, call or text with the URL, screenshots, and what must stay available.
Quick answers
Could this be my Wi-Fi?
Yes. Testing from cellular data helps separate a local connection problem from a public outage.
Who should own the domain?
The business should be able to access and manage its own registration.
Want it handled? IT Support — Something is broken? Tell us what stopped and what has to keep working.

Plain privacy and work terms: what we collect, how we keep it safe, and what gets written down before work starts.
What forms collect
Tech Audit and contact paths may collect your name, business name, contact information, follow-up preference, and a plain description of the issue. That is the minimum needed to reply usefully.
Who receives a form submission

Forms on this site are handled by Netlify, which hosts the site and stores each submission so Little Fight can read and reply to it. Nothing you send through a form is sold, and it is not used for advertising.

The Website Audit Lab is a separate tool with its own data flow — it takes a website address and an email address, and involves services this page does not cover. What the Audit Lab collects is written out separately.
Analytics
Little Fight uses Google Analytics, after consent, to understand which pages are useful and which contact paths work. Microsoft Clarity and the TikTok Pixel are not active on this site.

These tools may record page views, approximate device/browser details, referral information, and events such as phone clicks, email clicks, Tech Audit or contact button clicks, and form submits. Little Fight uses this information for measurement, reporting, and improving marketing, not to sell personal information.
Facebook and Instagram measurement

If you choose “Allow visits + Meta,” the Meta Pixel and Meta’s web Conversions API connection share public page views, contact clicks, inquiry starts, and confirmed form completions with Meta. It uses browser identifiers such as _fbp and _fbc, device information, IP address, and approved referral labels to measure which social visits lead to inquiries. This does not tell us the identity of every visitor or person who clicks.

We do not send form answers, names, email addresses, phone numbers, or private report links to Meta. Automatic advanced matching and automatic event collection are off. Meta may associate activity with its accounts and use it for personalized content and ads, under its privacy policy . You can manage Meta’s use in its “Activity from other businesses” settings.
Google Ads measurement

“Allow visits + Google Ads” lets Google Analytics share inquiry completion events with our linked Google Ads account. Approved campaign labels and Google click identifiers help connect an ad click with a later inquiry. Google may use first-party advertising cookies such as _gcl and _gac for this measurement. We do not send your form answers or contact details, upload customer lists, or enable Google ad personalization or remarketing.
Cookies, pixels, and opt-outs

Analytics is off by default for a first-time visitor. Google Analytics loads after a visit-counting choice. Google Ads and Meta each need their own explicit permission; allowing one does not grant permission to the other. An existing permission for the other service stays as you set it. “Allow visit counting” turns both advertising choices off. “Essential only” keeps all optional measurement off and the site still works. Global Privacy Control keeps both advertising choices off. Withdrawing advertising permission stops its measurement and removes the corresponding first-party advertising cookies; it does not erase data already received by a service. You can change your choice at any time using the footer.
What not to send
Do not send passwords, recovery codes, API keys, credit card numbers, bank details, protected health information, or private customer data through any public form on this site.
Work and scope

Project scope, pricing, access needs, and timelines are confirmed in writing before work begins. If anything changes mid-engagement, the change is written down and acknowledged before the work continues.
Safe account access

If access to a website, domain, payment tool, booking system, or business account is required, Little Fight sets up a safer handoff instead of asking for credentials over a public form, email, or text thread.
Privacy questions
For privacy questions or requests, email Little Fight at hello@littlefightnyc.com .

title: After Hours Agenda — Case Study | Little Fight NYC
heading: After Hours Agenda
description: A brand-led streetwear storefront that keeps product, payment, and made-to-order fulfillment connected.
metaDescription: A brand-led streetwear storefront that keeps product, payment, and made-to-order fulfillment connected.

contentBlocks.text: Custom storefront
By Little Fight NYC · Published 2026-05-13 · Updated 2026-08-19
The owner can put out a product drop in a day, and the store still looks like the brand.

A customer can choose a product, pay, and wait for shipping without seeing the machinery behind it, and the owner can put out a new drop in a day. After Hours Agenda is Little Fight NYC’s own streetwear experiment — the rare case where the agency is also the client, with all the dangers that brings. The brand was tight. The designs were ready. The audience was building. But the storefront was Shopify, and Shopify was flattening the brand. Every product page looked like every other Shopify product page, no matter what we put on it.

The choice was to keep patching a template or make a store that fit the brand from the start. We made the second one. Product details live in one place. Square takes payment. APLIIQ prints and ships, one order at a time. The owner does not have to babysit a pile of disconnected tools to put out a new drop.
The result is a storefront that looks like the brand instead of the platform. New product drops take a day, not a long rebuild.
The problem
A streetwear brand with a real point of view needed a real storefront. But Shopify’s templates were going to flatten everything that made the brand interesting.
What we kept
The brand identity, the product designs, and the voice — for the dreamers and the doers.
What we changed

Made one storefront that keeps product details together, sends payment through Square, and sends paid orders to APLIIQ for made-to-order printing and shipping. The owner does not have to rebuild the store for every drop.
What they got back
A storefront that looks like the brand, not like a Shopify theme. Payment and shipping have clear handoffs, and a new product drop can go out in a day.
Project at a glance
Custom — Built for the brand, not a template
1 day — To ship a new product drop
Square + APLIIQ — Payments + made-to-order fulfillment wired
Live site: afterhoursagenda.com
What you can count on

The first look is free. A website can be ready in six weeks or less when the scope and materials are agreed. The written plan names the scope, launch timing, what each side provides, and the care included. Urgent on-site help is a New York service; call so we can assess the issue and location, then confirm any on-site timing. A real person answers 9am–9pm Eastern. After hours, leave a message.

The way the work moves, not just the software you bought.
It matters when messages live in too many places, people copy the same details twice, or only the owner knows what happens next.
How it works

Start with one customer path: a message comes in, someone sees it, the work is scheduled or quoted, payment is recorded, and the next person can see the status. A business system makes those handoffs visible. It can use tools you already have; the useful part is agreeing where each step belongs.
A common situation

A neighborhood plumber gets calls, texts, and website forms. A simple system can put each new request in one shared list, show who owns the callback, and flag a quote that still needs a decision. The owner chooses the timing and message before any rule goes live.
The cost of ignoring it

Without a shared path, a callback can sit in a text thread, a quote can wait on an answer, and the work can live in one person’s memory. Count the requests that need a second ask in a normal week. That is a better starting point than a mystery benchmark.
Quick answers
Isn’t a business system just more software I have to learn?
No. It can be a shared checklist, a better intake form, or a clearer handoff between tools you already use. The goal is fewer places to check, not more apps to log into.
I’m a two-person shop. Am I too small for this?
No. A two-person shop may only need one clear list and a few agreed steps. Start when the same handoff keeps getting stuck, not because a vendor says it is time to upgrade.

How it works

A CRM gives each customer or lead one record. It can hold contact details, notes, status, and a next action. Some CRMs can create reminders or send messages, but the business still decides what information belongs there and who may see it.
A common situation

A contractor keeps inquiries in email, texts, and a spreadsheet. A CRM can put the customer name, job notes, estimate status, and next callback in one record. The team can agree which fields belong there before moving any existing list.
The cost of ignoring it

When customer details live in several places, people can repeat questions, miss a handoff, or lack the context to help. Before buying a CRM, check whether a shared list and a clear follow-up owner would solve the actual problem.
Quick answers
Do I need an expensive CRM like the big companies use?
Not automatically. Choose the smallest setup that supports the work you repeat. A fancy CRM that nobody opens is just a very expensive filing cabinet.
I already have my customers in a spreadsheet. Isn’t that enough?

A spreadsheet can be enough when it is current, shared appropriately, and has a clear owner. A CRM is worth considering when the team needs a repeatable next-action process or better context across several customer conversations.

A verified owner can update the profile information Google shows in Search and Maps. Keep the details accurate, use the official tools for verification and reviews, and check the current rules before changing anything. Google describes the profile and verification process in its own help center.
A common situation

A corner florist notices its profile still shows old holiday hours. The owner checks the official profile, corrects the hours, and makes sure the website and phone number match. That is a practical first fix; it does not promise a placement in search.
The cost of ignoring it

Wrong hours, location, or phone details can send a customer to the wrong place or stop them from reaching you. Start with the business facts you can verify; rankings and customer choices are not something anyone can promise.
Quick answers
Is this the same as having a website?

They do different jobs. A profile helps people find basic business details in Google; a website gives you more room to explain offers, show work, and choose the customer path. Which comes first depends on what the business needs.
How do I get more reviews without being pushy?

Ask for an honest review in a way that follows Google’s current review policies. Do not offer incentives or try to screen out unhappy customers. Check Google’s own rules before building a review request into a workflow.

All the apps you pay for, plus the work people still do around them.

How it works

List every tool, what it costs, who uses it, what data it holds, and what it connects to. Then ask three plain questions: does it support an important step, does the team use it, and is there a safer simpler option? Keep what earns its place. Change one thing at a time.
A common situation

A salon lists its booking app, payment system, newsletter tool, and spreadsheet. The owner can see which tool owns each task and where staff copy information by hand. That makes it possible to compare options without guessing that a new app will solve everything.
The cost of ignoring it

A messy stack can hide unused subscriptions, overlapping features, and manual re-entry. Review the statements and ask the team what they actually use before cancelling anything that might hold customer records or business history.
Quick answers
Does fixing my stack mean ripping everything out and starting over?

Usually not. Start with an inventory and one frustrating handoff. A replacement is worth considering only when the current tool cannot support a needed step, costs more than its value, or creates a real risk.
How do I know if I’m paying for tools I don’t use?

Compare recurring charges with a current list of tools and ask who uses each one. Check export options, contract terms, and stored data before cancelling. The forgotten login might be holding something important. Sneaky little goblins do that.

Workflow automation: The boring repeatable step happens without someone remembering to do it.
A rule that moves a routine step forward on its own. It can send a lead to the right place, create a follow-up task, or update a record.
The boring repeatable step happens without someone remembering to do it.
It matters when staff spend time copying details, chasing reminders, or checking three places to answer one question.
How it works

Automation is a simple “when this happens, do that” rule. For example: when a form comes in, add it to the shared list and create a follow-up task. Test the rule with a harmless example, decide who can see the data, and keep a person responsible for exceptions.
A common situation

A dog groomer wants appointment reminders to happen consistently. The business can test a reminder the evening before each appointment and keep an owner responsible for replies or changes. Whether it is worth keeping depends on the business’s own records and customer feedback.
The cost of ignoring it

Repeated copying and reminders can take attention away from customers, and a missed routine step can create extra cleanup. First measure the time and errors in one week. Automate only a step that is stable enough to trust.
Quick answers
Will automation make my business feel cold or robotic to customers?
It can, if it sends the wrong message or hides a real question. Automate the repeatable reminder; leave choices, exceptions, and conversation with a person.
Is this only for big companies with tech teams?
No. A small business can begin with one carefully tested rule. The right size depends on the task, the data involved, and who will own it after launch.

heading: Airtable vs. Notion vs. monday.com: Pick the Job First
description: Airtable organizes records. Notion organizes knowledge. monday.com organizes assigned work. Test the task your team needs to do.
metaDescription: Airtable organizes records. Notion organizes knowledge. monday.com organizes assigned work. Test the task your team needs to do.

contentBlocks.text: Airtable vs. Notion vs. monday.com: Pick the Job First
By Little Fight NYC · Published May 3, 2026 · Updated October 19, 2026
Airtable organizes records. Notion organizes knowledge. monday.com organizes assigned work. Test the task your team needs to do.
What this means for your business
All three can imitate each other. That does not make them equally comfortable. Pick the tool your staff can update during a busy day, not the one with the prettiest demo.
What to watch
The same fact copied into several tools.
A setup that only one person understands.
Guests, automations, storage, or permissions pushing the bill upward.
A dashboard that looks busy but changes no decision.
Do this next
Write the one job the tool must own.
Test that job with ten real records and two real users.
Price the plan you will need after the trial, not the free-plan fantasy.
Keep an export and name who owns the account.
What each job looks like in a real week

Lists of things that share the same details, like wholesale orders, catering inquiries, or equipment: that’s Airtable territory. Airtable suggests standalone forms as a way to let someone enter data without a full billable seat. People without an Airtable account can submit standalone forms shared with the “Anyone on the web” option. That suits part-timers who only add entries.
Pages people read and update now and then, like the opening checklist, the staff handbook, or vendor contacts: that’s Notion.
Jobs with an owner, a status, and a due date, like a renovation punch list or holiday prep: that’s monday.com.
Count editors and lookers separately

On paid plans, all three bill for full team seats: people with edit access in Airtable, and members in Notion and monday.com. All three also have a way to let someone look without adding to the bill. Count both groups before you choose.

Airtable: read-only collaborators and anyone using a shared view link don’t count toward the bill on its self-serve paid plans. On Team plans, Commenters are billable. Pick Read-only for someone who only needs to look.

Notion: adding a member to a paid workspace is billable. Guests get access to specific pages instead, up to your plan’s guest limit. Before you select Invite, hover over the person’s email address to confirm Notion is adding them as a guest, not a member. When Notion asks whether to upgrade a guest to a member, choose Skip for now to add them to that page at no cost.
monday.com: viewers can’t edit boards or content. monday.com says viewers don’t count toward billing. Members can edit, and how many you can invite depends on your plan.
When someone leaves, remove their access the same day. Here’s how to review who has access.
Test the way out before you build
Export your ten test records during the trial and open the file. If it’s messy now, it will be worse at a thousand.

Airtable: in a grid view, click the down arrow next to the view’s name, then Download CSV to get a spreadsheet file. A view is one saved layout of a table, and only what it shows gets exported, so use one with no filters and no hidden fields, or some records or columns get left out. Each table exports as its own file. Attachments come out as links that expire after a few hours, so keep the actual files somewhere the business owns.

Notion: go to Settings, select General under Workspace, then Export all workspace content. Notion emails you a download link. Pages the person exporting can’t access, like other people’s private pages, are left out. Notion also says you can’t instantly recreate a workspace by re-uploading the export.

If the team already runs fine on a shared spreadsheet, keep it. Move only when someone can name the step the new tool removes. If none of the three fits without workarounds, read when a custom system beats rented software.

description: Shopify leads when inventory and selling drive the business. Squarespace can fit a smaller catalog where content leads.
metaDescription: Shopify leads when inventory and selling drive the business. Squarespace can fit a smaller catalog where content leads.

contentBlocks.text: Shopify vs. Squarespace for a Local Shop
By Little Fight NYC · Published May 3, 2026 · Updated October 19, 2026
Shopify leads when inventory and selling drive the business. Squarespace can fit a smaller catalog where content leads.
What this means for your business
Start with how the shop sells. Where is stock recorded? What happens after an order? Who will update the site when a product sells out?
What to watch
Inventory updated separately online and in the shop.
A needed app or add-on for every ordinary task.
Shipping, returns, pickup, or taxes discovered after launch.
A redesign that breaks the path regular customers already use.
Do this next
Map one product from stock to sale to return.
List in-person, pickup, shipping, and marketplace needs.
Price the real plan, payment fees, apps, and hardware.
Test the full purchase on a phone before choosing.
Four checks that usually decide it

Selling at the counter. Both can run a point of sale (POS), the checkout at your counter. Shopify says that when you sell or restock a product on Shopify POS, the inventory count updates for that location. Squarespace says its Tap to Pay and Square Reader sales update inventory after every sale. Its Pay Link sales, paid through a link or QR code, need a manual stock update. Squarespace’s app also can’t be used with Square Register, Stand, or Terminal.

Delivery and pickup. Shopify can offer local delivery within a set distance of your shop or to certain ZIP codes. Squarespace offers local delivery by ZIP code, entered one at a time, plus local pickup. On Squarespace, customers can’t schedule a pickup time. If pickup is a big part of your day, test it in both.

Fast checkout buttons. Shopify says local delivery works with Shop Pay, but not with other fast checkouts like Apple Pay, Google Pay, Amazon Pay, or PayPal. If you deliver around the neighborhood, place a test order each way.

Catalog or story. If the site mostly answers hours, services, events, and photos, and the catalog is small, Squarespace may be all you need. If stock changes daily across sizes and colors, and the counter sells too, Shopify carries more of that load.
Keep a way out before you commit
Run a product export on day one, in whichever platform you pick, and open the file. In Squarespace, open the Products & Services panel, click Products, then Export all.

Know what the file leaves out. Squarespace’s product export skips featured images, variant images, image alt text, customer reviews, and additional product information. Keep the original product photos in a folder the business owns.
Keep the domain, the payment account, and the store login in the business’s name. Here’s how to own your domain name.

contentBlocks.text: When to leave the store alone

If orders come in, stock stays right, and staff can update products without calling anyone, keep the platform. A move means new links to redirect and a checkout regulars have to relearn. Fix the cheap things first: photos, product names, pickup instructions, and sold-out messages. Choosing a card reader too? See how to pick a POS system.
