title: Square Appointments vs. GlossGenius for Salons
heading: Square Appointments vs. GlossGenius for Salons
description: Compare the real booking path: staff, chairs, deposits, reminders, checkout, reports, and what clients see.
metaDescription: Compare the real booking path: staff, chairs, deposits, reminders, checkout, reports, and what clients see.

contentBlocks.text: Square Appointments vs. GlossGenius for Salons
By Little Fight NYC · Published May 3, 2026 · Updated October 19, 2026
Compare the real booking path: staff, chairs, deposits, reminders, checkout, reports, and what clients see.
What this means for your business
A booking tool owns more than a calendar. It touches service length, staff time, rooms or chairs, reminders, deposits, payment, and the return visit.
What to watch
Two calendars accepting the same time.
Staff, rooms, or chairs treated as unlimited.
Deposits and cancellation rules added outside the booking path.
Client details trapped in a system nobody can export.
Do this next
Write the most complicated real booking.
Build it in each trial, including deposit and reminder.
Run a cancellation, reschedule, checkout, and staff change.
Compare the plan and payment terms you actually need.
Where Square and GlossGenius actually differ
Both take online bookings, deposits, and card payments. The differences hide in a few settings. Check each one against how your salon books today.

Deposits on bookings your staff enter. Square says deposits are collected when a client books online. It does not currently take a deposit when you book for the client. GlossGenius says you can collect a deposit when you book by hand. It can text or email the client a payment link. The exception is a same-day appointment: GlossGenius says it can’t take a deposit on one you book by hand. If most bookings come by phone, text, or DM, start here.

Deposits on every plan. Square’s help lists deposits on its Free, Plus, and Premium plans. In Square Dashboard, the setting is under Appointments > Settings > Payments & cancellations. GlossGenius lists deposits as available on all subscription plans. You shouldn’t need an upgrade just to take a deposit.

Chairs, rooms, and stations. Square’s resource booking reserves a room, station, or chair with the service, so it can’t be double booked. Its help lists the feature for Square Premium subscribers. GlossGenius lists Room and Resource Management in its plan comparison, but not on its Standard plan.
Team size. GlossGenius plans differ in how many team members you can add. Check the plan comparison against your real headcount.

Cancellations after a deposit. Square says clients who paid a deposit can’t cancel on their own; the salon cancels for them. GlossGenius has clients acknowledge a non-refundable deposit policy when they book. You can still issue a refund in the app.
Before you switch, check what moves and what stays
A new booking tool costs more than its plan. Some things don’t make the trip.

Saved cards and photos stay behind. GlossGenius’s data transfer team says it can’t import client credit card details, client photos, past appointments and orders, gift cards, or deposit requirements on services. Expect regulars to re-enter a card. Keep your own list of open gift card balances.
Your client list can come along. The same team says it can import client contact information and notes, services, products, upcoming appointments, packages, and reviews.

Get your own copy first. Before you cancel anything, have the account owner export the client list from the current tool. Open the file and make sure names, phone numbers, and notes came through. If notes are missing, ask that tool’s support team for them before you cancel.

Add up a normal month, not the plan page. Add the subscription, card processing at the desk and online, deposits charged by card, and any card reader you’d replace. GlossGenius notes that deposits paid by card are subject to its payment processing fee. See how to cut monthly software costs.

links.text: how to cut monthly software costs

contentBlocks.text: When to keep the tool you have

Stay put if clients can book without calling, deposits land, and staff trust the calendar. A messy service menu or skipped settings is a cleanup job, not a reason to move. Fix the menu, turn on the deposit rule you already have, and book a test appointment on your phone. Switch when the tool can’t do something you need every week, like a deposit on phone bookings or a chair that keeps getting double booked.

title: Square vs. Toast for a Manhattan Restaurant
heading: Square vs. Toast for a Manhattan Restaurant
description: Pick the register and payment system around service: checks, courses, kitchen flow, online orders, offline plans, reporting, and support.
metaDescription: Pick the register and payment system around service: checks, courses, kitchen flow, online orders, offline plans, reporting, and support.

contentBlocks.text: Square vs. Toast for a Manhattan Restaurant
By Little Fight NYC · Published May 3, 2026 · Updated October 19, 2026
Pick the register and payment system around service: checks, courses, kitchen flow, online orders, offline plans, reporting, and support.
What this means for your business
A register and payment system change touches the busiest five minutes of the night. A feature list matters less than whether servers, kitchen staff, managers, online orders, and closeout agree.
What to watch
A demo that skips Friday-night volume.
Online orders retyped into the kitchen.
Hardware, payment, support, or contract terms left out of the quote.
No documented offline or outage procedure.
Do this next
Map dine-in, bar, takeout, delivery, and closeout.
Run the ten ugliest orders in each demo.
Compare the complete quote and contract, not a headline price.
Test offline steps and train staff before cutover.
Need a short way to frame the choice before you run a service test? Read the quick owner answer.
Hardware: what you keep and what you replace
Square’s restaurant page says hardware is not included with the subscription. It says you may be able to reuse iPads, kitchen printers, receipt printers, cash drawers, and routers.
Toast’s pricing page says its services only run on approved Toast hardware. Toast can change which devices it approves.
List every printer, cash drawer, tablet, and handheld you own today. Ask each vendor, in writing, which ones stay, which ones go, and what each device can do if you leave.
A Friday night without internet

Toast says cash and card payments still work in offline mode. Gift cards, loyalty redemptions, house accounts, and a few other payment types do not. Toast makes you responsible for declined, expired, or disputed offline payments, and strongly recommends getting devices back online within three days, preferably within 24 hours.

Toast devices can’t sync with each other offline, so an order taken on one terminal won’t show on the others. Toast recommends each employee stay on one device while offline. If the kitchen uses screens, Toast recommends a backup printer for the tickets those screens would show.

Square’s help center says Square Register, Terminal, and Handheld must upload offline payments within 72 hours, and highly recommends doing it within 24. Square’s card readers and stands stop taking offline payments after 24 hours until you reconnect. Pending offline payments expire after 72 hours and cannot be recovered. Square’s restaurant page uses the stricter 24-hour figure, so plan around 24. Square makes you responsible for expired, declined, or disputed offline payments. Square Gift Cards, Afterpay, Cash App Pay, Tap to Pay on a phone, and typed-in card numbers do not work offline, and older Square contactless readers (1st generation, v1 and v2) cannot take offline payments at all.

Ask both which payment types stop working offline. Then test it in both demos. Unplug the cable that brings internet into the modem and leave the router and Wi-Fi on, the way a real outage looks. Fire a course, split a check, and try a gift card. Reconnect and see what went through. In a real outage, do not delete or reinstall the app or reset a device that holds offline payments; Square adds signing out and switching modes or locations. Both say that can wipe those payments for good. If outages happen now, first check whether it is the internet or the Wi-Fi.

links.text: whether it is the internet or the Wi-Fi

contentBlocks.text: Leaving later: contracts and your data

Square’s restaurant page says its plans have no locked-in contracts. If you leave for another processor, Square’s help center says it can transfer your saved customer cards. Square says the transfer can take up to two weeks. The new processor must be PCI DSS Level 1 compliant. PCI DSS is the card industry’s security standard.
You can export the customer list in Square Dashboard under Customers > Customer directory > Directory, then Import / Export.

Toast’s help center says there is no single export of all your Toast data. Instead, you download reports from Toast Web, six months at a time, for up to the last 48 months. Toast says your data stays accessible for 60 days after you close the account.
Ask Toast for the full merchant agreement and its term before you sign. Ask Square which plan the quote assumes. Either way, pull a sample export in the first week, not the last.

If your current system gets through a full Friday and closes clean, a switch may not be worth the retraining. Fix the network and the menu setup first. Running a bar instead? See Toast vs. Clover for a bar.

title: How to Respond to Google Reviews | Little Fight NYC
heading: Reply to Google Reviews Like a Real Business
description: Keep replies short, specific, calm, and private. Thank good feedback, address the useful point, and move sensitive details offline.
metaDescription: Keep replies short, specific, calm, and private. Thank good feedback, address the useful point, and move sensitive details offline.

contentBlocks.text: Reply to Google Reviews Like a Real Business
By Little Fight NYC · Published July 12, 2026 · Updated October 19, 2026
Keep replies short, specific, calm, and private. Thank good feedback, address the useful point, and move sensitive details offline.
What this means for your business
Google says verified businesses can reply and those replies are public. A response can show that the business listens, but it cannot erase the review or prove who is right.
What to watch
Copy-paste replies that sound automated.
Customer, employee, order, health, or payment details in public.
Promises or admissions made while angry.
Incentives offered for changing or removing a review.
Do this next
Read the review once, then wait before replying if needed.
Thank the person or acknowledge the concern.
State one useful fact without arguing the whole case.
Offer the real private support channel when details are needed.
What happens after you post a reply
You need a verified profile to reply. In your Business Profile, select Read reviews, then Reply next to the review.
Google checks each reply against its content policies. Google says that usually takes up to 10 minutes but can take up to 30 days.
The reply shows as the business, not under your personal name.
The reviewer gets notified and can still change the review. You can edit or delete your reply later from the same Read reviews screen.
Google’s own reply tips add two points. Don’t use a reply to push deals or promotions. And don’t take the blame for things outside your control; say what you can and can’t do.
When a review breaks the rules
Report it instead of arguing in public. Google says only reviews that break its policies can be removed. It also says it doesn’t get involved in disputes between businesses and customers.
What counts: fake or paid reviews. Reviews with a conflict of interest count too, such as one from a current or former employee or a competitor.
How: in your Business Profile, select Read reviews, then Report next to the review. Pick a reason and send it.
Then wait. Google says evaluation typically takes several days. Track it in the Reviews Management Tool. If Google finds no violation, you get one appeal.

Someone posts bad reviews, then asks for money to take them down? Don’t pay. Save every message. Google has a separate report path for extortion scams involving negative reviews, linked from its page on reporting reviews.
Why a review isn’t showing up
Ask the customer if they can still see it, and save a screenshot. Then check Google’s list of reasons.
New reviews are checked against policy first. Google says that can delay them a few days.
After two profiles are merged, reviews from both can take a few days to show.
Customers on older phones may have trouble posting. Google suggests they update the Maps app. They must also be signed in to a Google Account, which can use a non-Gmail address.
Reviews removed for breaking policy won’t come back. If Google’s spam filter took down a real review, contact Google support. The same goes if reviews vanished after a profile was reinstated.
Ask for reviews without risking the profile
Google lets you share a review link or QR code, a square code customers scan with a phone camera. Put it on receipts, in a thank-you email or by the register.
Ask every customer, not only the happy ones. Google’s policy bars selectively asking for positive reviews.
No discounts, freebies or payment in exchange for a review.
Don’t pressure people to review while they are still in the shop. Don’t give staff a review quota or ask reviewers to name an employee.
Don’t ask staff or family to fill gaps. Google’s policy treats work and family ties as a conflict of interest.
Fixing the profile itself is a separate job. Here are Google Business Profile tips that follow Google’s rules.

We can fix the website and contact path a review exposed. Legal threats, harassment, or regulated complaints need qualified advice, not a clever reply.

title: Getting Into ChatGPT Answers: What You Can Control
heading: Getting Into ChatGPT Answers: What You Can Control
description: Publish current business facts and useful answers based on your work. Make the text easy for search engines to read, and keep your public profiles accurate.
metaDescription: Publish current business facts and useful answers based on your work. Make the text easy for search engines to read, and keep your public profiles accurate.

contentBlocks.text: Getting Into ChatGPT Answers: What You Can Control
By Little Fight NYC · Published July 12, 2026 · Updated October 19, 2026
Publish current business facts and useful answers based on your work. Make the text easy for search engines to read, and keep your public profiles accurate.
What this means for your business
ChatGPT search can use the web and show cited sources. Google says its AI search features rely on the same core search foundations. Neither service guarantees that it will mention your business.
What to watch
A vendor promising guaranteed AI placement.
Important information visible only after a click or inside an image.
Pages spun up for hundreds of tiny query variations.
Business facts that disagree across the website and profiles.
Do this next
Write the exact owner or customer question at the top.
Answer it plainly and add first-hand detail.
Cite external facts and link the appropriate service or action.
Keep public names, hours, locations, and offerings current.
First, make sure AI tools can read your site
Each AI search tool reads the web with a crawler. That is a program that reads your pages, like a new hire reading the menu. If your site turns it away, even a great page may not be cited.

ChatGPT. OpenAI says sites that opt out of OAI-SearchBot, its search crawler, will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers. It also says to check that your host or CDN allows traffic from OpenAI’s published addresses. A CDN is the service that delivers your site’s files.
Training is separate. OpenAI says you can block GPTBot, its training crawler, and still allow OAI-SearchBot for search.

Google. AI Overviews and AI Mode only link to pages that can already show in regular Google Search with a snippet, the short preview text under a result. Google also says your host and CDN should allow crawling, not just your robots.txt file.
Bing and Copilot. Microsoft says Copilot relies on the same crawling and indexing as regular Bing search. Its guidelines list blocking Bingbot in robots.txt as something to avoid.

A quick check: type your web address plus /robots.txt into a browser. OpenAI uses that public file to let site owners manage its crawlers. If OAI-SearchBot, Googlebot, Bingbot, or a lone * (which means every crawler) sits near a Disallow line, ask your web person what it blocks.
Skip the special AI tricks

Google says there are no extra requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode. You don’t need new machine-readable files or AI text files. You don’t need special hidden labels either: code that tells search engines facts like your hours without visitors seeing it. If your site already has those labels, Google says they should match the visible text on the page. Start with what Google looks for on a business website.

links.text: what Google looks for on a business website

contentBlocks.text: Some tricks can hurt. Bing warns that content designed to manipulate the language models behind Copilot may lead to reduced visibility or removal. So skip hidden notes written for chatbots.

Some vendors sell “AEO” or “GEO,” which Google describes as optimizing for AI experiences. Google suggests two questions for them. Does their advice match Google’s official guidance on AI features? Do they cite Google’s own documentation?
Check what the assistants say about you
Do this monthly, and after any change to hours or services. Ask what a customer would ask: your name plus “hours,” “walk-ins,” or your neighborhood.
In ChatGPT, type / and choose Search, then ask. Open Sources to see which pages it used. OpenAI says saved memories and your location can shape the search, so also try it signed out.
In Google, note whether an AI Overview appears and which links sit beside it. Google says AI Overviews often don’t show at all. A missing one is not a problem on its own.
Write down each wrong fact and the page it came from. Fix your website first. Then your Business Profile, which Google’s AI guide lists among the basics. Then outside listings you can edit.
Restaurants: OpenAI says ChatGPT may show reservation times from OpenTable, Resy, or Yelp, depending on the restaurant. Keep those listings as current as your site.

OpenAI says its search results and citations can be incomplete, outdated, or incorrect. You don’t control the answer, or every source it reads. You do control your website and the listings you can edit, so keep those right.

For Google, use Search Console, Google’s report on your search traffic. Google says clicks from AI Overviews and AI Mode are counted in its Performance report under “Web,” mixed in with regular search. It does not list them as a separate number.

We improve the pages and public details you control. Search and AI services decide what to show, so we do not promise a ranking or mention.

heading: The Best Small-Business Tech Is Quiet on Saturday
description: Reliable tools open, charge, book, print, back up, and recover. Excitement belongs in the business, not the login screen.
metaDescription: Reliable tools open, charge, book, print, back up, and recover. Excitement belongs in the business, not the login screen.

contentBlocks.text: The Best Small-Business Tech Is Quiet on Saturday
By Little Fight NYC · Published July 12, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026
Reliable tools open, charge, book, print, back up, and recover. Excitement belongs in the business, not the login screen.
What this means for your business
A feature is useful only when staff can operate it, the customer path still works, and someone can recover the account or data. Boring is a compliment when money is moving.
What to watch
One person is the only manual.
An outage plan that begins after the outage.
A tool added because a demo looked smart.
No export, backup, owner, support route, or replacement path.
Do this next
Write the five jobs that cannot stop.
Name the owner and backup operator for each.
Test offline, restore, recovery, and support steps.
Remove features that create more work than value.
What quiet looks like for each job

Start with the jobs customers notice first. For each one, a quiet setup answers four questions: who owns it, who runs it when that person is out, how it keeps working during an outage, and how it comes back after a mistake.

Taking payments: a second reader or a phone-based option, offline payment rules read before you need them, and card readers on the staff network, not the guest Wi-Fi. See what to check when a card reader drops.

links.text: what to check when a card reader drops

contentBlocks.text: Email: accounts in the business’s name, two people who can sign in as an administrator, and two-step sign-in with a backup method. See who should own business passwords.
Booking: a regular export of upcoming appointments, and a known way to reach customers if the booking tool goes down.
Files: one agreed home for shared files, a backup kept apart from the working copy, and a restore you have actually tried. See how to know files are really backed up.

links.text: how to know files are really backed up

contentBlocks.text: Phones: calls that ring the right people, voicemail someone checks, and the same number everywhere customers find you. See how to test a business phone number.

contentBlocks.text: Signs a tool is adding work

A new tool earns its place when it removes a step. Be wary when staff type the same details into two systems, when only one person knows how a setting works, or when a renewal arrives and nobody can say what the tool does. A yearly look at every paid tool catches most of these before they turn into a Saturday problem.
How to make a change without drama

Change one thing at a time, outside busy hours, with a way back. Test the job the change touches, then write down what changed and what to check first if something breaks. A plain note today makes the next problem faster to understand.

heading: Straight Answers to Small-Business AI Questions
description: Use AI for drafts, sorting, and low-risk assistance. Keep people responsible for private data, important facts, customer promises, and final decisions.
metaDescription: Use AI for drafts, sorting, and low-risk assistance. Keep people responsible for private data, important facts, customer promises, and final decisions.

contentBlocks.text: Straight Answers to Small-Business AI Questions
By Little Fight NYC · Published July 12, 2026 · Updated October 19, 2026
Use AI for drafts, sorting, and low-risk assistance. Keep people responsible for private data, important facts, customer promises, and final decisions.
What this means for your business
Choose one task before choosing an AI tool. What information would it need? What would a mistake cost? Who checks the result, and how would the team finish the work without it?
What to watch
Customer, employee, health, financial, legal, or credential data pasted into an unapproved tool.
An answer published without checking the source.
Automation sending a promise or decision to a customer.
A paid AI feature added before a real task is named.
Do this next
Choose one reversible, non-sensitive task.
Define the correct output and who reviews it.
Test with fake or public information.
Keep, change, or stop based on measured time and error, not hype.
Can staff paste customer details into ChatGPT?

Not into a personal account. There, chats stay in that person’s own history, outside the business’s control. If staff use one for work anyway, open Settings, then Data controls, and turn off Improve the model for everyone. OpenAI says new chats then won’t be used to train its models.
Two catches. OpenAI says a thumbs up or down on a reply can let that whole chat be used for training. That holds even after you opt out. And opting out does not delete saved chats.
OpenAI says it does not use content from ChatGPT Business or Enterprise workspaces to train its models by default. Even there, keep passwords, card numbers, and health details out.
Then give staff a three-line rule for a busy Saturday. What never goes in. Who checks the output. Who approves anything a customer will see.
We already pay for Google or Microsoft. Do we need another AI tool?
Maybe not. Plans change, so check what your current plan includes before you buy anything new.

Google says the Gemini app is now a core service for most Workspace editions. It says your content is not human reviewed or used to train AI models outside your organization without permission. That promise comes from your organization’s Workspace agreement, so staff should sign in with the work account.
Microsoft says prompts and responses in Microsoft Copilot for your organization, formerly Microsoft 365 Copilot, aren’t used to train the large models it runs on. Use the work sign-in there, too.

The bigger risk is your own sharing settings. Both companies say their assistant works with files a person already has permission to open. If everyone can open the payroll folder, the assistant can pull from it for everyone. Do a permission review first.
Can we use AI to screen job applicants in NYC?

Slow down. NYC’s Local Law 144 covers automated employment decision tools. That is the law’s term for certain software that helps make hiring or promotion decisions. Employers can’t use one unless it had a bias audit within the past year. A summary of the audit must be public. Candidates or employees must get the required notices. The city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection has enforced it since July 5, 2023.

If a hiring app offers AI ranking, ask the vendor for its bias audit before you turn it on. The city’s FAQ says the employer, not the vendor, is responsible for making sure the audit was done. Read the city’s AEDT page and FAQ, too. This summary reflects the city’s pages as of October 2026. It is not legal advice. Talk to an employment lawyer if you are unsure.
Can AI write our reviews?

No. The FTC’s rule on fake reviews, in effect since October 2024, covers reviews from people who don’t exist, “such as AI-generated fake reviews.” Businesses can’t create or sell them. The rule also bans rewards that depend on a review being positive or negative. This is a summary, not legal advice.
Using AI to draft a reply to a real review is different. Read the draft, fix it, and post it in your own words.

title: ADA Website Accessibility for NYC Small Businesses
heading: Website Accessibility: Fix Barriers, Not Just Scores
description: Keyboard access, labels, contrast, zoom, captions and manual testing matter. An overlay or a clean automated scan alone does not prove a site is accessible.
metaDescription: Keyboard access, labels, contrast, zoom, captions and manual testing matter. An overlay or a clean automated scan alone does not prove a site is accessible.

contentBlocks.text: Website Accessibility: Fix Barriers, Not Just Scores
By Little Fight NYC · Published July 12, 2026 · Updated October 19, 2026
Keyboard access, headings, labels, contrast, zoom, captions, errors, and real manual testing matter. An overlay or a clean automated scan alone does not prove a site is accessible.
What this means for your business

In its March 2022 web guidance, the U.S. Department of Justice says inaccessible web content can deny people equal access and lists practical considerations such as contrast, headings, keyboard use, and meaningful error cues. This page is not legal advice.
What to watch
Buttons or menus that need a mouse.
Forms with missing labels or unclear errors.
Text that cannot zoom or lacks contrast.
A clean automated score treated as proof of full accessibility.
Do this next
Test the main customer path with a keyboard and zoom.
Run automated checks and review the findings manually.
Fix blockers in forms, navigation, media, and purchase or booking flows first.
Create a way to report an accessibility problem and respond.
What the law says about a business website

The ADA covers businesses open to the public. Ada.gov lists examples such as retail stores, food and drink establishments, hotels, and medical offices. The Justice Department says the ADA’s requirements apply to what those businesses offer on the web, too.

Ada.gov’s web guidance, dated March 2022, says the Department has no regulation setting out detailed web standards. It says businesses can choose how they make online services accessible, but still must make them accessible. It points to WCAG as helpful guidance.
If someone says a 2024 federal rule sets your website standard, ask which rule. The April 2024 web requirements ada.gov mentions are for state and local governments.

New York City adds its own layer. When we checked in October 2026, the city’s business portal said businesses are public accommodations under the NYC Human Rights Law and must give patrons with disabilities reasonable accommodations unless that causes an undue hardship. It calls that law generally more expansive than state and federal law. That page does not set a website standard.
None of this is legal advice. If a demand letter or lawsuit arrives, call a lawyer before you reply or pay anyone.
The standard to ask your web person for

WCAG, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, is W3C’s standard for making web content more accessible to people with disabilities. Its success criteria come in three levels: A, AA, and AAA. W3C encourages using the latest version. It says content that meets WCAG 2.2 also meets 2.1 and 2.0.

So put WCAG 2.2 Level AA in the written scope. Start with the pages customers use most: home, menu or services, booking, checkout, and contact. Then cover the rest of the site. Ask how it will be tested, by hand as well as with tools.
A quick check you can run yourself

W3C publishes Easy Checks, a first review anyone can run in a browser. The steps below follow its 2023 version; W3C is drafting an update. It is quick, not final. W3C says a page can seem to pass and still have significant barriers.
Click the address bar, put the mouse aside, and press Tab to move through the page. Shift-Tab goes back. On a Mac, you may need to turn on keyboard navigation first.
Watch for a visible outline on whatever is selected. If you lose track of it, so will a keyboard user.
Make sure you can Tab out of anything you Tab into, like a video player. W3C calls getting stuck a “keyboard trap.”

Go through a booking or checkout without the mouse, up to the last confirm or pay button. If you do finish one, cancel or refund it after. W3C flags features that only work on mouse hover as a common problem.
Make the text 200% bigger. W3C says badly built pages show overlapping sections or text that disappears.

Be skeptical of a widget that promises to make your site compliant on its own. In April 2025, the FTC approved a final order against accessiBe. It bars the company from claiming its automated products can make any website WCAG-compliant without evidence to support that.

title: Calendly vs. Square Appointments: Meeting or Service?
heading: Calendly vs. Square Appointments: Meeting or Service?
description: Calendly centers on meetings. Square Appointments connects service booking, staff, resources, deposits, and payment. Start with the actual appointment.
metaDescription: Calendly centers on meetings. Square Appointments connects service booking, staff, resources, deposits, and payment. Start with the actual appointment.

contentBlocks.text: Calendly vs. Square Appointments: Meeting or Service?
By Little Fight NYC · Published July 12, 2026 · Updated October 19, 2026
Calendly centers on meetings. Square Appointments connects service booking, staff, resources, deposits, and payment. Start with the actual appointment.
What this means for your business
Both can put time on a calendar. The difference appears after the click: what gets reserved, whether money moves, what staff need, and how the client returns.
What to watch
A meeting tool stretched into chairs, rooms, classes, or service inventory.
A service platform bought for simple introductory calls.
Two tools both writing availability.
Reminders, payment, cancellation, and follow-up handled in separate manual steps.
Do this next
Write the most complicated real appointment.
Name calendars, staff, resources, deposit, checkout, and reminders.
Build and cancel that appointment in each trial.
Compare the plan and payment terms needed for the complete flow.
What each one actually reserves

Calendly builds around event types, which are reusable meeting templates. It has four: one-on-one, group, collective (several hosts meet one invitee), and round robin (meetings rotate across a team). Group and collective start on Calendly’s Standard plan; round robin needs Teams or Enterprise.

That fits time with a person: a consult, a call, a walkthrough. In Square Appointments, an appointment is booked with a client and stands for a service to be performed. Its payment rules sit in the same system. If clients book a cut, a treatment, or a lesson, start there. If they book a conversation, a meeting tool is usually enough.
Money: when the client pays and who refunds

Calendly connects to Stripe or PayPal, and its help center lists payments on paid plans, not the free plan. On a paid event type, the client pays during booking, and the meeting is confirmed once the payment goes through. The money goes straight to your Stripe or PayPal account, and refunds happen there, not in Calendly.

Square Appointments sets booking payment rules in Square Dashboard under Appointments > Settings > Payments & cancellations. You pick one of three: no requirement, full prepayment for fixed-price services, or hold a card in case of a no-show.

Square says enforcement and refunds on prepaid appointments are up to you. Whether clients can cancel a prepaid booking online depends on your settings: if you let clients cancel or reschedule online, they can; if you also accept or decline requests, they have to contact you once you accept. You can charge a cancellation fee up to 14 days after the appointment. Refunds for cancellations more than 60 days after booking have to be issued outside Square. A card held for no-show protection covers that one appointment, unless the client chooses to save it.
Square’s help article lists these settings for Square Appointments Plus and Premium subscribers. Check the current plans before you count on them.
Let one calendar run the show

Calendly checks connected calendars for busy times and adds each new meeting to one main calendar you choose. The free plan connects one calendar; paid plans connect up to six per user. Connected calendars apply to every event type, so you can’t send different kinds of meetings to different calendars.

Square Appointments can import from Google Calendar, export to it, or both. Busy Google events block time on the appointments calendar. Only appointments go to Google, and only personal events come back to Square. Square warns against adding events to the synced appointments calendar from Google, because a re-sync can wipe them. Square lists Google sync for its Plus and Premium subscribers too.

Pick one tool to own availability. Book a test from each side, cancel it, and check both calendars. For the full routine, see how to stop double bookings. Running a salon? Compare Square Appointments vs. GlossGenius.

heading: QuickBooks vs. Wave: Ask the Bookkeeper First
description: Wave can fit simpler books. QuickBooks can fit broader accounting workflows and accountant expectations. Tax needs and clean records decide.
metaDescription: Wave can fit simpler books. QuickBooks can fit broader accounting workflows and accountant expectations. Tax needs and clean records decide.

contentBlocks.text: QuickBooks vs. Wave: Ask the Bookkeeper First
By Little Fight NYC · Published July 12, 2026 · Updated October 19, 2026
Wave can fit simpler books. QuickBooks can fit broader accounting workflows and accountant expectations. Tax needs and clean records decide.
What this means for your business
Accounting software is a record system, not just an invoice template. Your business type, sales tax, payroll, inventory, entities, bank feeds, and professional support change the fit.
What to watch
Choosing before asking the person who closes the books or files taxes.
Features assumed from an old plan comparison.
Historical records with no clean export.
Payment, payroll, or bank-feed fees left out of total cost.
Do this next
Ask the bookkeeper or accountant which records and reports they require.
List payroll, inventory, sales tax, projects, payments, and users.
Compare current official plans and total fees.
Test export, reconciliation, and year-end handoff before migrating.
Questions to ask your bookkeeper or accountant first
Ask before you sign up or switch. Their answers usually settle it.
Which one do you already work in? A system they don’t know can mean slower, costlier month-ends.

Do you need your own login? In QuickBooks Online, only a primary admin or company admin can invite users. They go to Settings ⚙ > Manage users > Accountants or Accounting Firms > Invite firm. Intuit says an accountant invited this way doesn’t count toward your user limit. In Wave, inviting someone as an Admin, Editor, or Viewer takes Wave’s Pro Plan.

Do you count stock? Wave says it does not track the unit value of inventory. You record inventory by its dollar value. You also update cost of goods sold, the account for what the sold items cost you, by hand with a journal entry, a bookkeeping adjustment. Wave says you can do that after each sale or in bulk at the end of a period. If you need item counts, check which QuickBooks plan includes inventory tracking, and ask your accountant how they would set it up.
Who files? Software can calculate sales tax and payroll tax. Ask who actually files, pays, and answers the state when a notice arrives.
Payroll in New York: ask what gets filed, not just paid
Running paychecks is the easy part. Ask which New York filings the payroll service pays and files for you.
Wave’s help is a good example. It lists these New York payroll taxes as ones Wave pays and files:
New York State, New York City, and Yonkers withholding.
State unemployment and the New York Reemployment Fund.
The Metropolitan Commuter Transportation Mobility Tax (MCTMT).

Wave says it only calculates New York State Disability Insurance (SDI) and New York Family Leave Insurance (FLI). It does not pay or file those. Wave also says tax payments and filings are part of its full access payroll subscription.
Ask QuickBooks Payroll, or any payroll service, the same question in writing. Then confirm with your accountant who handles disability and paid family leave.
Get the records out before you change anything

Leaving QuickBooks Online: Intuit says that after you cancel, you have read-only access to your data for one year. A former paid subscriber can export to Excel up to a year after canceling. Intuit still recommends exporting or printing before you cancel. Do that.
Leaving Wave: among invited users, Wave’s permissions table gives data export to Admins only. Editors, Payroll Managers, and Viewers can’t run it, so the export may be on you.

Check who owns each account. In Wave, the owner is the person whose email was used to sign up, or the current primary email on the account. In QuickBooks, check who holds the primary admin role. It should be the business, not a past bookkeeper. See who should own the passwords.
If your accountant is happy, the bank feed works, and year-end goes smoothly, stay where you are. If you do move, let your accountant pick the cutover date so the old and new books meet cleanly.

The logo on the terminal is not the whole system. Hardware, payment processing, apps, support, network, contract, replacement timing, and closeout all matter when the room is full.
What to watch
A quote that leaves out processor, reseller, app, hardware, or support terms.
Tabs, tips, modifiers, printers, or offline steps skipped in the demo.
Support responsibility split among several companies.
A cutover scheduled without staff training or fallback.
Do this next
Write ten ugly rush-hour orders and the nightly close.
Run them on the exact hardware and plan quoted.
Read payment, term, cancellation, support, and replacement terms.
Document network, offline, cash, and escalation procedures.
Tabs and the nightly batch
A pre-authorization is a hold placed on a guest’s card when the tab opens. The batch is the day’s card sales, sent off so you get paid. In a bar open late, the two run into each other.

Toast says a pre-authorization lasts 24 hours. Pre-authorized checks do not close on their own. Toast says to close them before the auto-batch time, typically 4 a.m. Any still open then are voided. If you pour until 4, ask Toast how your batch time is set.
Toast says a guest with enough money for the hold, but not the full check, gets declined at close-out. Toast also says a tapped chip card does not put the guest’s name on the tab; dipping does.

Clover’s auto-closeout sends the day’s card sales for processing during a 50-minute window. Clover says to enter paper tips 50 minutes before your closeout time. If closeout runs first, Clover says the unentered tips are lost; its support can add them by hand, but that delays the batch’s deposit. Some owners and admins can change the closeout time in the dashboard; if not, Clover support changes it.
Test it on both: open a tab at 1 a.m., add rounds, leave a paper tip, and close it after your real last call.
When the internet drops mid-rush

For tabs, Toast says new pre-authorizations do not work in Offline Mode. A card pre-authorized before the outage can still close a check, and that payment waits in a queue until the device is back online. Regular card payments still work offline. Toast says you are responsible for declined, expired, or disputed offline payments, lets you set a dollar limit above which an offline card payment needs a manager, and strongly recommends getting devices back online within three days, preferably within 24 hours. Toast also warns that uninstalling the app or clearing the device memory permanently deletes stored payments.

Clover sets offline payments device by device. You can cap each offline payment and the total a device takes offline. Clover says devices can take offline payments for up to 7 days, and you accept the risk of a declined or partial payment. Clover also warns not to uninstall the app while offline, because that deletes the offline payments.

Ask each vendor which payment types stop working offline and who carries a decline. Then test it in each demo: unplug the cable that brings internet into the modem and leave the router and Wi-Fi on, the way a real outage looks. Open a tab on one terminal and look for it on another. Run a card, print a ticket, reconnect, and check what went through. If drops happen now, first check whether it is the internet or the Wi-Fi.

contentBlocks.text: Who sold it to you decides how you leave

Clover is sold directly and through banks and other partners. Its pricing page says contract terms and termination fees vary by that provider. It also says Clover devices bought or leased from other sellers cannot be used with other payment processors. So the seller’s contract, not the logo on the screen, sets your exit.

Toast’s billing FAQ says you must use Toast’s processing services, and no other processor can run alongside it. If you switch to Toast, you must cancel the old processor yourself. Ask both for the full agreement, the seller’s legal name, and the term before you sign.
If your bar already closes clean on either system, keep it. Fix the network and the tab routine before you pay to switch.

title: The Pool Room | The Lab · Little Fight NYC
heading: The Pool Room
description: A New York dive bar built in Blender: 2,229 objects, 90 materials, visible-source lighting, and a 240 Hz physics-solved break with collision-timed sound.
metaDescription: A New York dive bar built in Blender: 2,229 objects, 90 materials, visible-source lighting, and a 240 Hz physics-solved break with collision-timed sound.

contentBlocks.text: We built a bar that doesn’t exist. Then broke a rack in it.
Open the audio-described film (MP4, 23 MB). The original collision audio remains underneath concise spoken descriptions of every shot.
0:00–0:05 — Inside the dark bar, the camera looks through a diamond-latticed window at wet Lower East Side storefronts and a backwards neon OPEN sign. Quiet room tone plays.
0:05–0:10 — The camera glides along rows of bottles, an old register, and fluorescent sections that stop on either side of it.
0:10–0:14 — A low view passes a foamy pint, condensation on the glass, and a rocks cocktail resting on its coaster.
0:14–0:19 — The view crosses the room and lowers past the three-shade fixture toward green cloth, a cue ball, and fifteen tightly racked balls.
0:19–0:23 — The cue strikes. Balls scatter with rapid clacks; the 7 ball and then the 4 ball fall into the southeast corner pocket.
0:23–0:27 — The camera follows the 13 ball, the last one moving, until its final rail contacts fade and it stops.
0:27–0:30 — The camera rises and pulls back over the settled table, booths, bar, overhead fixture, and lit storefront. Quiet room tone remains.
What you’re looking at
Every object in this room was made from scratch. The bar, the booths, the register, the 213 bottles behind it. No cameras, no photos, no stock.

The balls are not keyframed. A physics simulation worked out where they go, and every sound sits on a simulated collision. This is a showroom build, not a client space, client result, or real-world promise.
Spec
Room
Table
Regulation 9-foot
Ball
Solver
240 Hz
Renderer
Cycles, path-traced
Lights with a real source
Objects in the frozen environment
Authored materials
Physics contracts passing
Playback parity checks
Worst orientation error, any frame
Breaks simulated to choose one
The room
It had to look like somebody drinks here.
Rooms read as real through small things. Every light has a fixture you can point at. Nothing floats. It’s worn, not dirty. We checked all 1,127 objects for whether something actually holds them up.
01 One fixture over the table, and real air between it and the far wall.
02 The sign reads backwards because you’re inside it.
03 Mismatched stools. Nobody buys them all at once.
04 An aisle narrow enough to make you turn sideways.
05 The shelves split around the register, because a machine that size wouldn’t fit otherwise.
06 Wiped for this shift. The age is worn finish, not grime.
07 Somebody’s tab, mid-drink.
08 Two booths, bolted to the wall.
09 Cracked vinyl at arm height, where arms go.
10 Twenty years of paste. Four corners have lifted enough to cast their own shadow.
11 Somebody put a daylight bulb in the cage, so the hall runs cold.
12 One tube in the room runs at 70%. Tired, not dead.
The break
Not animated. Solved.
Tell the physics where the cue ball sits, how hard it’s hit and where the tip lands, and it works out the rest: 248 collisions over 7.8 seconds. We didn’t place a single one.
Then we checked it. 216 tests confirm what you see matches the physics on every frame, to within a fifteenth of a degree.
We simulated 90 different breaks and threw out 26 — scratches, weak racks, balls left blocking a pocket. This is the best of the 64 that were legal.
13 Nine foot. The nap is worn where people lean.
14 Fifteen balls, 57.15 mm each, racked tight.
15 Cue-ball height, the way you’d actually sight it.
Cue ball at impact
Solver events in one break
Rail contacts before it settles
Balls down — the 4 and the 7
Until nothing is moving
240 Hz
Trajectory sample rate
The sound
Every sound sits on a real hit.
Nothing was timed by ear. Each clack is placed on the collision that caused it, and how hard it lands comes from how fast the balls were actually moving.
In the first fiftieth of a second, 99 balls hit each other . That pile-up is the sound of a break.
What this means for you
If it doesn’t exist yet, we can still show it.

A space you have not built. A product you have not manufactured. A machine that would be dangerous to film. We can make an illustrative study to test how an idea may look or move. It is not a construction, product, or performance guarantee.

title: Privacy — VERA
heading: Your hunt stays yours.
description: VERA has no accounts, ads, or analytics. Hunt state stays in your browser; optional address checks go directly to NYC Planning.
metaDescription: VERA has no accounts, ads, or analytics. Hunt state stays in your browser; optional address checks go directly to NYC Planning.

contentBlocks.text: Privacy
Your hunt stays yours.

VERA has no accounts, advertising, analytics, or lead resale. Your saved hunt stays in this browser. If you choose to check an exact address, that address goes directly from your browser to NYC Planning’s GeoSearch service — not to Little Fight NYC.
Effective 8 August 2026 · VERA is operated by Little Fight NYC

The short version. We do not ask who you are, set a VERA cookie, or run analytics or advertising scripts. Saved listings, notes, viewing checklists, preferences, commute anchors, income, and confirmed address matches live in your browser’s local storage. The optional address checker sends only the address you type directly to NYC Planning so you can confirm the building.
What we collect
No first-party profile. There is no sign-up, email field, account, or password. Little Fight NYC does not receive your saved hunt, notes, income, commute anchors, or address-check query.

Our web host (Netlify) produces standard server logs — IP address, timestamp, requested file, user agent — as an automatic function of serving any website. We do not link those to a person, do not use them to build a profile, and do not sell or share them. They exist for security and uptime.
What stays on your device
VERA writes the following workspace state to localStorage :
vera-cases — the listings you saved, the stage you put each one in, your notes, and your viewing-checklist ticks.
vera-workspace — your filter preferences, so the console opens where you left it.
vera-anchors — up to two subway stations you chose as commute anchors.
vera-profile — the annual income you entered for the local 40× qualification check.
vera-address-resolutions-v1 — a building match you explicitly confirmed, including its label, confidence, BBL or BIN, and confirmation time.
That saved workspace data is not synced, backed up, or read back by Little Fight NYC. It is tied to one browser on one device, and clearing site data erases it permanently.
The optional address check

Some public listings omit or blur the exact building. If you submit an address in VERA’s confirmation form, your browser requests up to three possible matches from the official NYC Planning GeoSearch service. The request omits browser credentials and the referring page. NYC Planning still receives the address and normal connection data, such as your IP address and user agent, under its own privacy practices.

Nothing is saved until you choose a candidate. The selected label, match confidence, BBL or BIN, and timestamp then stay in this browser. The confirmation does not alter VERA’s shared feed, score, ranking, or owner grade.
What we publish

The console reads one sanitised public feed through littlefightnyc.com/vera/data/public.json . Before anything is published, the pipeline removes the private research layer — contact names, phone numbers, email addresses, working notes, and internal watch-list state — and neutralises subjective language about named owners. Building records, violation counts, litigation counts, and rent-stabilisation status remain because they come from public records.
Where the data comes from

VERA indexes rental listings that are already publicly posted, and enriches them with New York City and State public records — including Housing Preservation and Development violation history, Department of Buildings records, housing-court signals, and rent-stabilisation registries. It displays selected published listing facts and photos for analysis and links every record back to its original source.
Third parties

VERA makes only the network requests needed to operate: Netlify serves the site and its first-party public-feed endpoint and may log requests; GitHub hosts the sanitised publication behind that endpoint and may receive normal proxy request metadata; OpenFreeMap supplies map tiles; and listing-photo hosts receive image requests when published photos appear. Your browser does not contact a separate VERA host. Those photo requests suppress the VERA page referrer, but the image host still receives normal connection data such as your IP address and user agent. NYC Planning receives an address only when you submit the optional address check. Clicking an original listing takes you to that publisher’s site and privacy practices.
There is no advertising network, tag manager, analytics script, session recorder, social widget, or font CDN in VERA. Its typefaces are served from Little Fight NYC.
Your rights

There is no VERA account to export, correct, or delete. You control the hunt data stored in your browser and can clear it at any time. A confirmed building match also includes a Forget this address control so you can remove it without clearing the rest of your hunt. If you have a question about this policy, contact Little Fight NYC through the main site .
Changes

If this policy changes materially, the effective date above changes with it. Any future change that introduced accounts, first-party personal-data collection, or behavioral tracking would require a visible product and policy change; we would say so plainly.

title: Field manual — VERA
heading: Field manual
description: New York rent law in hard numbers, sixteen scam tells, and the 26-point viewing checklist — free, no account, from the VERA apartment engine.
metaDescription: New York rent law in hard numbers, sixteen scam tells, and the 26-point viewing checklist — free, no account, from the VERA apartment engine.

contentBlocks.text: Field manual
New York rent law in hard numbers, sixteen scam tells, and the 26-point viewing checklist — free, no account, from the VERA apartment engine.
The money, by law
Security deposit: capped at 1 month (HSTPA 2019), returned within 14 days of move-out, itemized.
Screening fee: the actual cost or $20, whichever is less — waived with a qualifying credit or background report from the last 30 days.

Extra fees: for a standard residential rental, a landlord cannot demand an extra holding, reservation, or key fee before or at the beginning of the tenancy. Lawful rent and up to one month of security may still be due under the lease.
Broker fee: a broker representing the landlord, or publishing their listing with permission, cannot charge you; a broker you independently hire can (FARE Act, in effect since June 11, 2025).
Income convention: 40× monthly rent annually; guarantors are asked for 80×.
Read the law itself
NYS fee and screening rule — Application, screening, and pre-tenancy payment limits in Real Property Law §238-a.
NYC broker-fee rule — DCWP’s current FARE Act guidance and complaint path.
HCR rent-history access — Who can obtain a rent history and how HCR delivers it.
HCR lease rider — The required rider/addendum for stabilized vacancy and renewal leases.
NYC stabilization guide — Why building age and size are clues, not a complete status determination.
Scam School — the sixteen tells
The price is good but not absurd

The professional version never uses a $1,400 West Village one-bedroom. It shaves 15% off market — cheap enough to move fast, plausible enough to survive a gut check. Compare against the building’s own last-rented price, not your hopes.
Nobody has proven they own it

The most expensive scams in this city all collapse to one unanswered question: is this person the owner, the managing agent, or a stranger with a set of keys? A real tour and a real-looking lease prove neither. Look the owner up before you look at the apartment.
One phone number, thirty listings
Search the phone number and the email. Scaled operations reuse contact details across dozens of listings under different names in different neighborhoods. One search ends it.
A lease that looks completely legitimate
A DocuSign lease requires no verification of the sender. Renters have signed real-looking leases, wired real money, and arrived to find twenty other people with the same lease for the same unit.
"I am out of the country"
Missionary, oil rig, deployment, sick relative abroad. Same script for a decade, usually paired with "view it through the windows and we will mail the keys."
Extra money before the tenancy

For a standard residential rental, the landlord cannot demand an extra holding, good-faith, reservation, or key fee before or at the beginning of the tenancy. Lawful rent and up to one month of security may still be due under the lease. Get every amount itemized and reject off-the-books extras.
Zelle, Venmo, wire, gift cards
Irreversible by design — that is the entire reason they were requested. A real landlord takes a check or an ACH transfer against a signed lease.
"You hired me by emailing me"

The most common FARE Act dodge. It does not work: publishing a listing creates a legal presumption the landlord authorised the broker, and conditioning a rental on engaging an agent is barred outright.
A cheaper rent with a bigger fee
Offered a choice between $4,250 rent with a $3,600 fee, or $3,800 rent with a $6,840 fee? That is not a favour, it is fee laundering — and the owner often has no idea their rent is being quoted high.
An application fee over $20

Credit and background checks cost the actual cost or $20, whichever is less. Bring a qualifying credit or background report from the last 30 days and the fee must be waived. A "$500 processing fee" is not a red flag, it is illegal.
A tip for the super
Key money by another name. A demand for a few hundred dollars "for the super" before move-in is illegal, and brokers who ask for it know exactly what they are doing.
"Let us just talk on the phone"
Insisting on a call after you asked in writing is a paper-trail problem, not a friendliness problem. Keep every fee conversation in text or email.
Days on market reset to three
The same tired unit gets relisted — sometimes with the unit number flipped from #A1 to #1A — to wipe the counter. Four months of sitting reappears as brand new inventory.
The listing is already rented
Plenty of live listings are pure lead bait. "Oh, that one is gone, but I have something similar" is a sales funnel, not an accident.
A virtual doorman is not a doorman
Neither is a shared courtyard a "private outdoor space." Amenity checkboxes are filled in to win filters, not to describe the apartment.
Net effective rent
The advertised number is often after a free month. Judge the lease on gross rent — the net figure is mostly a promise to raise your rent at renewal.
The viewing checklist
Systems
Run the shower AND the sink together — Pressure dies in old buildings when two fixtures compete.
Time the hot water — Over a minute to warm up is a boiler that will fail you in February.
Find the radiator valve — Steam heat with no working valve means a 85° apartment all winter with the windows open.
Check for an AC sleeve or window that fits a unit — Some leases and some windows make a summer unit impossible.
Count outlets in every room — Two outlets per room means extension cords forever.
Damage
Look up — ceiling stains or fresh paint patches — A fresh white square on an old ceiling is a leak someone painted over.
Open the cabinet under the sink — Roach traps, droppings, and water damage all live under there.
Check corners and baseboards for gaps — Gaps are mouse highways. Steel wool is a tell someone already fought this.
Set a pen on the floor — If it rolls, the building has settled — check the walls for cracks too.
Light + air
What is actually outside each window — Airshaft and brick-wall views are legal and soul-crushing.
Which way do the windows face — North-facing means no direct sun, ever.
Open and lock every window — Painted-shut windows are both a comfort and a fire-safety problem.
Life
Stand still and listen for 60 seconds — Bar, bus line, elevated train, upstairs dog — all invisible at 2pm on a Tuesday.
Check phone bars in the back room — Thick pre-war walls kill signal. Ask if the wifi provider is a monopoly here.
Ask where packages land — No mailroom and a street-level door means porch piracy every week.
Laundry in the building? Where is the nearest one? — A five-block laundromat walk is a real weekly tax.
Find the trash area and smell it — You will be walking past it every day.
People
Knock on a neighbor door and ask about the landlord — Thirty seconds with a neighbor beats any listing description.
Ask if there is a super and how fast they answer — The difference between a same-day fix and a three-week outage.
Paper
Confirm this is THE unit, not "a similar one" — Bait-and-switch is the oldest move in the book.
Is it a legal unit? (basement/cellar especially) — Illegal conversions have no protection and can be vacated by the city.

If it may be stabilized, ask for the rent-stabilization rider — A stabilized vacancy or renewal lease must include the state rider. Missing it is a reason to verify the unit — not proof that the unit is unregulated.

Ask the outgoing tenant for the rent history — HCR treats rent histories as confidential: it releases them to the legal tenant, owner, or an authorized representative. The history is mailed to the apartment, so an outgoing tenant can share theirs; once you are the legal tenant, request your own.
Notice if the rent is an odd number — A rent like $1,187.59 rather than a round $1,200 is a classic sign of a regulated increase calculated off a legal rent.

Read who pays the broker, in writing — Under the FARE Act, a landlord-hired broker cannot bill you a fee. Keep the fee conversation in text or email — a sudden insistence on a phone call is about the paper trail.
Verify it yourself
Who Owns What — See every other building the same owner controls. Free, open source, and the tool New Yorkers recommend to each other most.
HPD Online — Violations by class, complaints, and the registered owner. Class C means immediately hazardous.
ACRIS — The deed and the mortgage. Confirms who actually owns the building — and whether the asking rent could plausibly carry it.
DOB Building Information — Permits, complaints, and the Certificate of Occupancy that tells you whether the unit is even legal.
NY licence check — Every real broker holds a licence. Search the name before you send anything.
311 complaint history — Heat and hot water outages by date. A building that lost heat five times last winter will do it again.

title: Terms — VERA
heading: An instrument, not an agent.
description: Terms of use for VERA: a research instrument, not a broker, not a listing service, and not legal advice.
metaDescription: Terms of use for VERA: a research instrument, not a broker, not a listing service, and not legal advice.

contentBlocks.text: Terms of use
An instrument, not an agent.
VERA reads public listings and public records, scores what it finds, and shows its work. It does not represent you, does not represent a landlord, and does not take a cut of anything.
Effective 4 August 2026 · VERA is operated by Little Fight NYC
What VERA is

A research and analysis tool for people looking for an apartment in New York City. It aggregates listings that are already publicly posted, cross-references the addresses it can resolve against available public records, and presents an opinionated evaluation with the reasoning attached.
What VERA is not
Not a real-estate broker or agent. It is not licensed, it does not show apartments, negotiate, or represent either side of a transaction, and it earns nothing from any lease you sign.
Not a listing service. It does not host inventory. Every listing links back to its original source, which is the authority on price, availability, and terms.

Not legal advice. Where these pages describe New York rent law, that is general information, current to the best of our knowledge on the effective date above, and it is not a substitute for a tenant attorney or a housing counsellor.
Not financial advice. The calculators are arithmetic on figures you supply and on common landlord conventions. They are not an assessment of what you can afford.
Accuracy, and the limits of it

Listing data is only ever as good as its source, and rental listings are frequently stale, duplicated, mispriced, or fabricated. VERA is explicitly built around that fact — it scores authenticity, flags what it could not verify, and clusters duplicates — but it cannot guarantee that any listing is real, available, accurately priced, or legally rentable.

Public-record enrichment depends on matching a listing’s address to a building record. That match can fail or land on the wrong building. Where confidence is low, VERA says so. Treat every score as a starting point for your own verification, never as a conclusion. Verify the unit, the landlord, and the lease in person and in writing before you pay anyone anything.

If you use the optional exact-address check, the address you type goes directly from your browser to NYC Planning’s GeoSearch service. You must choose and verify the returned building match yourself. A local confirmation does not change the shared listing, score, ranking, or owner grade.

Nothing here should be the last thing you check. A high score means VERA found no problems in the data it can see. It cannot see the water pressure, the neighbours, or the person you are about to hand a deposit to.
Acceptable use
Use VERA for your own NYC apartment search, or to help someone you know, on a non-commercial basis.
Do not scrape, mirror, or resell the published data, or use it to build a competing commercial index.
Do not use it to harass, profile, or target any landlord, owner, or occupant. Public records describe buildings, not people to pursue.
Do not present VERA’s evaluations as your own professional opinion to a third party.
Ownership

The VERA name, mark, interface, scoring system, and written content are the property of Little Fight NYC. Underlying public records remain the property of the agencies that publish them. Listing content belongs to whoever posted it.
Liability

VERA is provided as-is and without warranty of any kind, express or implied, including any warranty of accuracy, availability, or fitness for a particular purpose. To the fullest extent permitted by law, Little Fight NYC is not liable for any loss arising from your use of the tool or reliance on its output — including any rental decision, deposit, application fee, or lease you enter into.
You are responsible for your own housing decisions. That is not a disclaimer we are hiding behind; it is the honest description of a tool that reads records and hands you the reading.
Availability

VERA publishes on a nightly cadence and may be stale, incomplete, or offline at any time. There is no uptime commitment and no support obligation. Sources break; when they do, the System page shows the available source status rather than quietly presenting a thinner city as complete.
Changes
These terms may change; the effective date above will change with them. Continued use after a change constitutes acceptance.
Contact
Questions about these terms go to Little Fight NYC via the main site .
Grades, corrections, and fair housing

Steward grades and verification signals are computed from cited public records; each reported failure names its source where it appears. Owners and agents can report a wrong join or misreading via the corrections page ; disputes with the underlying record must be corrected with the publishing agency before a later sweep can reflect them. VERA never uses race, religion, national origin, familial status, disability, source of income, or any protected characteristic in scoring or curation; neighborhood focus reflects the active search brief, not a judgment about who should live anywhere.

title: Brand kit — VERA
heading: VERA looks like the instrument it is.
description: The VERA brand kit: mark, wordmark, palette, semantic colour rules, typography, and voice.
metaDescription: The VERA brand kit: mark, wordmark, palette, semantic colour rules, typography, and voice.

contentBlocks.text: Brand kit
VERA looks like the instrument it is.

A rental-intelligence system earns trust by looking calm, precise, and visibly capable. VERA can carry restrained luminous depth and a more futuristic premium finish, but every layer stays in service of the record: colour means one thing at a time, and the interface never performs confidence it has not earned.
Version 2.1 · maintained by Little Fight NYC
The mark

A constructed V made from three open planes. It can read as a folded map, an open record, or a building seen in elevation — the layers VERA brings together: place, evidence, and decision. One short green seam marks the verified path. The mark is fixed; it never scans, spins, or loops.
PRIMARY LOCKUP · DARK
PRIMARY LOCKUP · LIGHT
Rules
Clear space — keep the height of the mark free on every side of the lockup.
Minimum size — 24 px for the mark alone, 88 px wide for the full lockup.
The verification seam is always green. Never recolour it to match a campaign.
The wordmark is IBM Plex Serif 600 at 0.14em tracking. Never set it in the sans or mono, never italicise it, and never letter-space it further.
Never enclose the lockup in a box other than the app icon, where the container is a 25% rounded square.
Palette

Warm black, not blue-black — the interface is meant to feel like a room at night rather than a terminal. Restrained low-contrast gradients, translucent glass, and fine hairlines may create hierarchy and depth; they must never compete with a status colour or disguise the boundary between fact and interpretation. Everything else is signal.

The semantic rule that matters most: green means this is good or this is selected . Amber means we do not know yet . Red means we checked and it is bad . Luminous depth may come from neutral surfaces, glass, gradients, and hairlines — never by borrowing a semantic colour for decoration. If a colour is ever used for any other reason, the interface starts lying, and every future signal gets cheaper.
Typography

Three voices, all IBM Plex. The serif gives editorial judgment and key decisions a human cadence; the sans carries explanation and interface language; the mono carries anything a machine produced — identifiers, timestamps, counts, coordinates, and labels. The shift tells a reader whether VERA is interpreting, explaining, or measuring.
The record stays beside the decision.
Clean buildings, private landlords
When an address resolves cleanly, VERA checks it against available city records and labels what remains unknown.
NEEDS VERIFICATION
Voice
VERA is the friend who reads the lease. Plain, specific, unsentimental, and never cheerful about bad news. It says what it knows, says what it does not, and never pads either.
Do
“Only seen on a single source — verify independently.”
“An application fee over $20 is not a red flag, it is illegal.”
“Nothing clears the bar under this lens.”
Name the number, then explain it.
Don’t
“Amazing deal — act fast!”
“Oops! Something went wrong 😅”
“No results found.” (Say what was actually searched.)
Never dress an empty state as a failure. Empty is an answer.
Motion

Motion exists to show causality and system response — a number stepping because a filter changed, a route indicator moving to the active workspace, a panel rising because it opened, or a focused record resolving into the next layer of evidence. It can feel crisp, premium, and quietly futuristic, but never ornamental: no decorative loops, no ambient attention traps, no neon soup. Every transition is interruptible, obeys prefers-reduced-motion , and carries no information that the still interface withholds.
The name

VERA — Verified Evaluation for Rental Analysis. Set in caps, never “Vera”, never possessive in product copy. Referred to as “it”, not “she”: it is an instrument, and pretending otherwise would be the first dishonest thing it does.

title: Corrections — VERA
heading: Corrections
description: How VERA uses public records to grade buildings, and how to report a wrong record or a mistake in the way VERA reads it.
metaDescription: How VERA uses public records to grade buildings, and how to report a wrong record or a mistake in the way VERA reads it.

contentBlocks.text: Corrections

VERA calculates its building grades from public records. These include HPD housing violations and complaints, DOB building records, and 311 heat and hot-water complaints. It also uses bedbug filings under Local Law 69 and HPD building litigation records. Each issue shown with a grade links to its source.
If you own or manage a graded building

If a city record is wrong, ask HPD or DOB to correct it. This might involve a cleared violation, a resolved complaint, or a current registration. Once the agency publishes its update, a later VERA check can read the new record.

Think VERA has the wrong building or reads a record incorrectly? Email hello@littlefightnyc.com with the address and the claim you want checked. Little Fight reviews how VERA matched and read the public record. We fix confirmed mistakes in that process. If the agency record itself is wrong, that agency must correct it before VERA can show an update.
What VERA will not do

VERA never contacts owners, never solicits, and never removes accurate public records from view. No one edits a grade by hand. VERA calculates it again after a record is matched or read correctly, or after the source record changes. A payment, relationship, or request cannot change a grade.
Fair housing

VERA scores buildings and listings from public records and listing data only. It never uses race, religion, national origin, familial status, disability, source of income, or any protected characteristic in scoring or curation. Neighborhood focus reflects the active search brief — not a judgment about who should live anywhere.

title: Privacy | Little Fight NYC Website Audit Lab
heading: We only ask for what the audit needs.
description: Privacy information for the Little Fight NYC Website Audit Lab, including what the audit collects and how report emails are used.
metaDescription: Privacy information for the Little Fight NYC Website Audit Lab, including what the audit collects and how report emails are used.

contentBlocks.text: Privacy
We only ask for what the audit needs.

The Website Audit Lab asks for a public website URL and an email address for the report. Do not send passwords, private documents, payment details, recovery codes, or account access through this audit.
What we collect
The public website URL submitted for the audit.
The email address used to send the report.
Technical audit results for the submitted public page.
Business details inferred from that public page, such as the company name, business category, city, and state.
How we use it
The email address is used to send the audit report and, when appropriate, follow up about fixing the issues found. Little Fight NYC does not sell audit submissions.
What the audit does not need

The Website Audit Lab does not need logins, passwords, recovery codes, payment details, private files, customer records, staff records, API keys, or access to business accounts. It reviews public website information and technical signals that are already visible from the outside. If a deeper project later requires access to a website, Google profile, hosting account, booking tool, or payment platform, Little Fight will walk through a safer access method outside this public form.
Report delivery and follow-up

The report is sent to the email address provided. Little Fight may use that email to follow up about the report, ask a practical clarification, or suggest the free Tech Audit when the page problem appears connected to a larger website, search, software, lead, booking, payment, or workflow issue. The point is clarity, not pressure.
Public website testing

The submitted page may be tested for speed, mobile experience, search basics, accessibility signals, trust cues, and customer-path friction. The report is not legal, financial, security, medical, accessibility, or compliance advice or certification. It is a first look that can help an owner decide whether a focused fix or wider review makes sense. For the public standards behind common checks, read Chrome Lighthouse documentation , W3C accessibility guidance , and HHS HIPAA information .
Optional analytics

If you previously chose “Allow visit counting” on Little Fight NYC, Google Analytics receives this page path and bounded funnel events such as audit started, accepted, ready, or a broad failure category. Those events never include the website address, email address, audit ID, report URL, or provider error text. With “Essential only” or no choice, the Audit Lab does not load Google Analytics or send these events.
How long we keep it

The generated report and its related viewing data are scheduled for deletion after 30 days. Little Fight keeps a minimal follow-up record with the email address, public business details, report link, and delivery status. The active follow-up record is scheduled for deletion 12 months after submission. Netlify Pro scheduled backups are retained for 30 days, and on-publish backups retain the last 10 production publishes. Those recovery copies can outlive active deletion. You may ask us to delete the active follow-up record sooner. Read Netlify’s privacy notice for its own handling terms.

When Little Fight approves a non-production deploy for testing, Netlify may create an isolated database copy for that branch. New audit submissions in non-production do not create durable follow-up records, and the isolated copy is removed with the branch.
Who else handles it
Running the audit means a few named services see part of a submission. Nothing is sold, and no one on this list receives more than what is described here.
Netlify : hosts the site, runs the audit, and stores the report and limited follow-up record. Read Netlify’s privacy notice .

Google : PageSpeed Insights receives the submitted public URL for technical testing. Google Workspace and Gmail receive the recipient address and report email for delivery. With analytics consent, Google Analytics receives only the bounded event data described above. Read Google’s privacy policy .
Anthropic : may receive public page text and technical signals through Netlify AI Gateway to help write the findings. The email address is not sent to Anthropic. Read Anthropic’s privacy policy .
Each is a business tool under Little Fight’s own account, used to deliver the report and follow up on it, and each is governed by its own privacy terms.
Data requests

Questions or deletion requests about an audit submission can be sent to Little Fight NYC at the contact details below. Include the website URL and email address used for the report so the request can be matched to the right submission.
Questions
Email hello@littlefightnyc.com or call (646) 360‑0318 .

Archive note: This supplied biography is historical reference material, not independently verified current information. It stays here only to show the interface study.
Concert + Festival Promoter

Mike Ziemer began interviewing bands and reviewing albums for online magazines in 2002. The work gave him a way into shows and a chance to meet his favorite artists. A local band later asked him to manage them. His first task was to put on a concert in the suburbs.

In March 2004, Third String Productions was born at The Plano Centre where Ziemer would hold shows in multiple rooms from 2004-2009 with attendance ranging from 500 to 4,800. The Plano Centre was the birthplace of Unsilent Night and So What?! Music Fest .
After outgrowing the Plano Centre, Ziemer began booking live events across Texas and beyond, averaging as many as 400 events annually between multiple markets from 2021-2023.

In 2022, Third String Entertainment formed a strategic joint venture with Disco Donnie Presents, named Disco Punk , to further grow the So What?! Music Festival brand. 2023's festival was the largest in the festival's history bringing in over 22,000 people across 2 days in Dallas, TX.
Ziemer is also a partner in Furnace Fest , taking place annually in Birmingham, AL featuring a wave of bands primarily from the late 90s and early 2000s hardcore and post-hardcore scene.

Over the last 20 years, Ziemer has been instrumental in helping introduce and build artists through his festivals including A Day To Remember, Enter Shikari, Forever The Sickest Kids, Dance Gavin Dance, Beartooth, Of Mice & Men, Polyphia , and many more.
Other Ventures

Ziemer has also independently run his own record label, Third String Records since 2014. The label has released music for over a dozen bands with streams totaling over 20 million across all platforms.

He also founded the artist management company, Flip A Switch Music Group alongside his partners Luke Knipe and Matt Dunne. The management company roster currently includes songwriters, producers, engineers, and bands.

During 2020, while live music was on pause, Ziemer opened up his first recording studio, Flip A Switch Studios in his backyard of his Oak Cliff home. In 2021, he opened his second recording studio in Deep Ellum. The studios have attracted some of Texas' hottest acts including Bashfortheworld, Tay Money, Lil Twist, SVDDEN DEATH, Luna Luna, LilBootyCall, and many more.
Supplied 2023 photo captions. This gallery does not show recent posts.
This is a supplied snapshot of venture cards, not a current portfolio or availability list.
So What?! Music Festival

Since 2007, So What?! Music Festival has taken place 15 times in Texas including 10 spring editions, 2 fall editions, 1 Houston edition, and 2 summer editions. The "go to" festival for metal / hardcore / pop punk / emo fans.
Furnace Fest

Originally taking place from 2000-2003, Furnace Fest was revived in 2021 as a resurrection of the event. Taking place annually in Birmingham, AL featuring bands from the late 90s and early 2000s hardcore and post-hardcore scene.
Monster Mosh Music Festival
Originally taking place in 2008-2009, Monster Mosh regained popularity in 2022 when it returned as a mini-festival at Gilley's in Dallas. In 2023, the festival expanded to 2 days.
Restless Fest / Restless Shows
Founded in 2023 by Mike Ziemer, Restless Fest is a music festival with heavy emphasis on next-gen music.
Flip A Switch Studios
Founded in 2020, offering affordable recording services in Deep Ellum and Oak Cliff.
Flip A Switch Music Group
A management company with offices in Los Angeles and Dallas.
Flip A Switch Creative
A full service agency with emphasis on creating "fear of missing out."
